# mockall/lib.rs

[1](https://docs.rs#1)// vim: tw=80
[2](https://docs.rs#2)//! A powerful mock object library for Rust.
[3](https://docs.rs#3)//!
[4](https://docs.rs#4)//! Mockall provides tools to create mock versions of almost any trait
[5](https://docs.rs#5)//! or struct. They can be used in unit tests as a stand-in for the real
[6](https://docs.rs#6)//! object.
[7](https://docs.rs#7)//!
[8](https://docs.rs#8)//! # Usage
[9](https://docs.rs#9)//!
[10](https://docs.rs#10)//! There are two ways to use Mockall.  The easiest is to use
[11](https://docs.rs#11)//! [`#[automock]`](attr.automock.html).  It can mock most traits, or structs
[12](https://docs.rs#12)//! that only have a single `impl` block.  For things it can't handle, there is
[13](https://docs.rs#13)//! [`mock!`].
[14](https://docs.rs#14)//!
[15](https://docs.rs#15)//! Whichever method is used, the basic idea is the same.
[16](https://docs.rs#16)//! * Create a mock struct.  It's name will be the same as the original, with
[17](https://docs.rs#17)//!   "Mock" prepended.
[18](https://docs.rs#18)//! * In your test, instantiate the mock struct with its `new` or `default`
[19](https://docs.rs#19)//!   method.
[20](https://docs.rs#20)//! * Set expectations on the mock struct.  Each expectation can have required
[21](https://docs.rs#21)//!   argument matchers, a required call count, and a required position in a
[22](https://docs.rs#22)//!   [`Sequence`].  Each expectation must also have a return value.
[23](https://docs.rs#23)//! * Supply the mock object to the code that you're testing.  It will return
[24](https://docs.rs#24)//!   the preprogrammed return values supplied in the previous step.  Any
[25](https://docs.rs#25)//!   accesses contrary to your expectations will cause a panic.
[26](https://docs.rs#26)//!
[27](https://docs.rs#27)//! # User Guide
[28](https://docs.rs#28)//!
[29](https://docs.rs#29)//! * [`Getting started`](#getting-started)
[30](https://docs.rs#30)//! * [`Static Return values`](#static-return-values)
[31](https://docs.rs#31)//! * [`Matching arguments`](#matching-arguments)
[32](https://docs.rs#32)//! * [`Call counts`](#call-counts)
[33](https://docs.rs#33)//! * [`Sequences`](#sequences)
[34](https://docs.rs#34)//! * [`Checkpoints`](#checkpoints)
[35](https://docs.rs#35)//! * [`Reference arguments`](#reference-arguments)
[36](https://docs.rs#36)//! * [`Reference return values`](#reference-return-values)
[37](https://docs.rs#37)//! * [`impl Trait`](#impl-trait)
[38](https://docs.rs#38)//! * [`Mocking structs`](#mocking-structs)
[39](https://docs.rs#39)//! * [`Generic methods`](#generic-methods)
[40](https://docs.rs#40)//! * [`Generic traits and structs`](#generic-traits-and-structs)
[41](https://docs.rs#41)//! * [`Associated types`](#associated-types)
[42](https://docs.rs#42)//! * [`Multiple and inherited traits`](#multiple-and-inherited-traits)
[43](https://docs.rs#43)//! * [`External traits`](#external-traits)
[44](https://docs.rs#44)//! * [`Static methods`](#static-methods)
[45](https://docs.rs#45)//! * [`Modules`](#modules)
[46](https://docs.rs#46)//! * [`Foreign functions`](#foreign-functions)
[47](https://docs.rs#47)//! * [`Debug`](#debug)
[48](https://docs.rs#48)//! * [`Async Traits`](#async-traits)
[49](https://docs.rs#49)//! * [`Crate features`](#crate-features)
[50](https://docs.rs#50)//! * [`Examples`](#examples)
[51](https://docs.rs#51)//!
[52](https://docs.rs#52)//! ## Getting Started
[53](https://docs.rs#53)//! ```
[54](https://docs.rs#54)//! use mockall::*;
[55](https://docs.rs#55)//! use mockall::predicate::*;
[56](https://docs.rs#56)//! #[automock]
[57](https://docs.rs#57)//! trait MyTrait {
[58](https://docs.rs#58)//!     fn foo(&self, x: u32) -> u32;
[59](https://docs.rs#59)//! }
[60](https://docs.rs#60)//!
[61](https://docs.rs#61)//! fn call_with_four(x: &dyn MyTrait) -> u32 {
[62](https://docs.rs#62)//!     x.foo(4)
[63](https://docs.rs#63)//! }
[64](https://docs.rs#64)//!
[65](https://docs.rs#65)//! let mut mock = MockMyTrait::new();
[66](https://docs.rs#66)//! mock.expect_foo()
[67](https://docs.rs#67)//!     .with(predicate::eq(4))
[68](https://docs.rs#68)//!     .times(1)
[69](https://docs.rs#69)//!     .returning(|x| x + 1);
[70](https://docs.rs#70)//! assert_eq!(5, call_with_four(&mock));
[71](https://docs.rs#71)//! ```
[72](https://docs.rs#72)//!
[73](https://docs.rs#73)//! ## Static Return values
[74](https://docs.rs#74)//!
[75](https://docs.rs#75)//! Every expectation must have an associated return value (though when the
[76](https://docs.rs#76)//! **nightly** feature is enabled expectations will automatically return the
[77](https://docs.rs#77)//! default values of their return types, if their return types implement
[78](https://docs.rs#78)//! `Default`.).  For methods that return a `static` value, the macros will
[79](https://docs.rs#79)//! generate an `Expectation` struct like
[80](https://docs.rs#80)//! [`this`](examples::__mock_MockFoo_Foo::__foo::Expectation).
[81](https://docs.rs#81)//! There are two ways to set such an expectation's return value: with a
[82](https://docs.rs#82)//! constant
[83](https://docs.rs#83)//! ([`return_const`](examples::__mock_MockFoo_Foo::__foo::Expectation::return_const))
[84](https://docs.rs#84)//! or a closure
[85](https://docs.rs#85)//! ([`returning`](examples::__mock_MockFoo_Foo::__foo::Expectation::returning)).
[86](https://docs.rs#86)//! A closure will take the method's arguments by value.
[87](https://docs.rs#87)//!
[88](https://docs.rs#88)//! ```
[89](https://docs.rs#89)//! # use mockall::*;
[90](https://docs.rs#90)//! #[automock]
[91](https://docs.rs#91)//! trait MyTrait {
[92](https://docs.rs#92)//!     fn foo(&self) -> u32;
[93](https://docs.rs#93)//!     fn bar(&self, x: u32, y: u32) -> u32;
[94](https://docs.rs#94)//! }
[95](https://docs.rs#95)//!
[96](https://docs.rs#96)//! let mut mock = MockMyTrait::new();
[97](https://docs.rs#97)//! mock.expect_foo()
[98](https://docs.rs#98)//!     .return_const(42u32);
[99](https://docs.rs#99)//! mock.expect_bar()
[100](https://docs.rs#100)//!     .returning(|x, y| x + y);
[101](https://docs.rs#101)//! ```
[102](https://docs.rs#102)//!
[103](https://docs.rs#103)//! Additionally, constants that aren't `Clone` can be returned with the
[104](https://docs.rs#104)//! [`return_once`](examples::__mock_MockFoo_Foo::__foo::Expectation::return_once)
[105](https://docs.rs#105)//! method.
[106](https://docs.rs#106)//!
[107](https://docs.rs#107)//! ```
[108](https://docs.rs#108)//! # use mockall::*;
[109](https://docs.rs#109)//! struct NonClone();
[110](https://docs.rs#110)//! #[automock]
[111](https://docs.rs#111)//! trait Foo {
[112](https://docs.rs#112)//!     fn foo(&self) -> NonClone;
[113](https://docs.rs#113)//! }
[114](https://docs.rs#114)//!
[115](https://docs.rs#115)//! # fn main() {
[116](https://docs.rs#116)//! let mut mock = MockFoo::new();
[117](https://docs.rs#117)//! let r = NonClone{};
[118](https://docs.rs#118)//! mock.expect_foo()
[119](https://docs.rs#119)//!     .return_once(move || r);
[120](https://docs.rs#120)//! # }
[121](https://docs.rs#121)//! ```
[122](https://docs.rs#122)//!
[123](https://docs.rs#123)//! `return_once` can also be used for computing the return value with an
[124](https://docs.rs#124)//! `FnOnce` closure.  This is useful for returning a non-`Clone` value and also
[125](https://docs.rs#125)//! triggering side effects at the same time.
[126](https://docs.rs#126)//!
[127](https://docs.rs#127)//! ```
[128](https://docs.rs#128)//! # use mockall::*;
[129](https://docs.rs#129)//! fn do_something() {}
[130](https://docs.rs#130)//!
[131](https://docs.rs#131)//! struct NonClone();
[132](https://docs.rs#132)//!
[133](https://docs.rs#133)//! #[automock]
[134](https://docs.rs#134)//! trait Foo {
[135](https://docs.rs#135)//!     fn foo(&self) -> NonClone;
[136](https://docs.rs#136)//! }
[137](https://docs.rs#137)//!
[138](https://docs.rs#138)//! # fn main() {
[139](https://docs.rs#139)//! let mut mock = MockFoo::new();
[140](https://docs.rs#140)//! let r = NonClone{};
[141](https://docs.rs#141)//! mock.expect_foo()
[142](https://docs.rs#142)//!     .return_once(move || {
[143](https://docs.rs#143)//!         do_something();
[144](https://docs.rs#144)//!         r
[145](https://docs.rs#145)//!     });
[146](https://docs.rs#146)//! # }
[147](https://docs.rs#147)//! ```
[148](https://docs.rs#148)//!
[149](https://docs.rs#149)//! Mock objects are always `Send`.  If you need to use a return type that
[150](https://docs.rs#150)//! isn't, you can use the
[151](https://docs.rs#151)//! [`return_const_st`](examples::__mock_MockFoo_Foo::__foo::Expectation::return_const_st),
[152](https://docs.rs#152)//! [`returning_st`](examples::__mock_MockFoo_Foo::__foo::Expectation::returning_st),
[153](https://docs.rs#153)//! or
[154](https://docs.rs#154)//! [`return_once_st`](examples::__mock_MockFoo_Foo::__foo::Expectation::return_once_st),
[155](https://docs.rs#155)//! methods. If you need to match arguments that are not `Send`, you can use the
[156](https://docs.rs#156)//! [`withf_st`](examples::__mock_MockFoo_Foo::__foo::Expectation::withf_st)
[157](https://docs.rs#157)//! These take a non-`Send` object and add runtime access checks.  The wrapped
[158](https://docs.rs#158)//! object will be `Send`, but accessing it from multiple threads will cause a
[159](https://docs.rs#159)//! runtime panic.
[160](https://docs.rs#160)//!
[161](https://docs.rs#161)//! ```
[162](https://docs.rs#162)//! # use mockall::*;
[163](https://docs.rs#163)//! # use std::rc::Rc;
[164](https://docs.rs#164)//! #[automock]
[165](https://docs.rs#165)//! trait Foo {
[166](https://docs.rs#166)//!     fn foo(&self, x: Rc<u32>) -> Rc<u32>;   // Rc<u32> isn't Send
[167](https://docs.rs#167)//! }
[168](https://docs.rs#168)//!
[169](https://docs.rs#169)//! # fn main() {
[170](https://docs.rs#170)//! let mut mock = MockFoo::new();
[171](https://docs.rs#171)//! let x = Rc::new(5);
[172](https://docs.rs#172)//! let argument = x.clone();
[173](https://docs.rs#173)//! mock.expect_foo()
[174](https://docs.rs#174)//!     .withf_st(move |x| *x == argument)
[175](https://docs.rs#175)//!     .returning_st(move |_| Rc::new(42u32));
[176](https://docs.rs#176)//! assert_eq!(42, *mock.foo(x));
[177](https://docs.rs#177)//! # }
[178](https://docs.rs#178)//! ```
[179](https://docs.rs#179)//!
[180](https://docs.rs#180)//! ## Matching arguments
[181](https://docs.rs#181)//!
[182](https://docs.rs#182)//! Optionally, expectations may have argument matchers set.  A matcher will
[183](https://docs.rs#183)//! verify that the expectation was called with the expected arguments, or panic
[184](https://docs.rs#184)//! otherwise.  A matcher is anything that implements the [`Predicate`] trait.
[185](https://docs.rs#185)//! For example:
[186](https://docs.rs#186)//!
[187](https://docs.rs#187)//! ```should_panic
[188](https://docs.rs#188)//! # use mockall::*;
[189](https://docs.rs#189)//! # use mockall::predicate::*;
[190](https://docs.rs#190)//! #[automock]
[191](https://docs.rs#191)//! trait Foo {
[192](https://docs.rs#192)//!     fn foo(&self, x: u32);
[193](https://docs.rs#193)//! }
[194](https://docs.rs#194)//!
[195](https://docs.rs#195)//! let mut mock = MockFoo::new();
[196](https://docs.rs#196)//! mock.expect_foo()
[197](https://docs.rs#197)//!     .with(eq(42))
[198](https://docs.rs#198)//!     .return_const(());
[199](https://docs.rs#199)//!
[200](https://docs.rs#200)//! mock.foo(0);    // Panics!
[201](https://docs.rs#201)//! ```
[202](https://docs.rs#202)//!
[203](https://docs.rs#203)//! See [`predicate`] for a list of Mockall's builtin predicate functions.
[204](https://docs.rs#204)//! For convenience,
[205](https://docs.rs#205)//! [`withf`](examples::__mock_MockFoo_Foo::__foo::Expectation::withf)
[206](https://docs.rs#206)//! is a shorthand for setting the commonly used
[207](https://docs.rs#207)//! [`function`] predicate.  The arguments to the predicate function are the
[208](https://docs.rs#208)//! method's arguments, *by reference*.  For example:
[209](https://docs.rs#209)//!
[210](https://docs.rs#210)//! ```should_panic
[211](https://docs.rs#211)//! # use mockall::*;
[212](https://docs.rs#212)//! #[automock]
[213](https://docs.rs#213)//! trait Foo {
[214](https://docs.rs#214)//!     fn foo(&self, x: u32, y: u32);
[215](https://docs.rs#215)//! }
[216](https://docs.rs#216)//!
[217](https://docs.rs#217)//! # fn main() {
[218](https://docs.rs#218)//! let mut mock = MockFoo::new();
[219](https://docs.rs#219)//! mock.expect_foo()
[220](https://docs.rs#220)//!     .withf(|x: &u32, y: &u32| x == y)
[221](https://docs.rs#221)//!     .return_const(());
[222](https://docs.rs#222)//!
[223](https://docs.rs#223)//! mock.foo(2 + 2, 5);    // Panics!
[224](https://docs.rs#224)//! # }
[225](https://docs.rs#225)//! ```
[226](https://docs.rs#226)//!
[227](https://docs.rs#227)//! ### Matching multiple calls
[228](https://docs.rs#228)//!
[229](https://docs.rs#229)//! Matchers can also be used to discriminate between different invocations of
[230](https://docs.rs#230)//! the same function.  Used that way, they can provide different return values
[231](https://docs.rs#231)//! for different arguments.  The way this works is that on a method call, all
[232](https://docs.rs#232)//! expectations set on a given method are evaluated in FIFO order.  The first
[233](https://docs.rs#233)//! matching expectation is used.  Only if none of the expectations match does
[234](https://docs.rs#234)//! Mockall panic.  For example:
[235](https://docs.rs#235)//!
[236](https://docs.rs#236)//! ```
[237](https://docs.rs#237)//! # use mockall::*;
[238](https://docs.rs#238)//! # use mockall::predicate::*;
[239](https://docs.rs#239)//! #[automock]
[240](https://docs.rs#240)//! trait Foo {
[241](https://docs.rs#241)//!     fn foo(&self, x: u32) -> u32;
[242](https://docs.rs#242)//! }
[243](https://docs.rs#243)//!
[244](https://docs.rs#244)//! # fn main() {
[245](https://docs.rs#245)//! let mut mock = MockFoo::new();
[246](https://docs.rs#246)//! mock.expect_foo()
[247](https://docs.rs#247)//!     .with(eq(5))
[248](https://docs.rs#248)//!     .return_const(50u32);
[249](https://docs.rs#249)//! mock.expect_foo()
[250](https://docs.rs#250)//!     .with(eq(6))
[251](https://docs.rs#251)//!     .return_const(60u32);
[252](https://docs.rs#252)//! # }
[253](https://docs.rs#253)//! ```
[254](https://docs.rs#254)//!
[255](https://docs.rs#255)//! One common pattern is to use multiple expectations in order of decreasing
[256](https://docs.rs#256)//! specificity.  The last expectation can provide a default or fallback value,
[257](https://docs.rs#257)//! and earlier ones can be more specific.  For example:
[258](https://docs.rs#258)//!
[259](https://docs.rs#259)//! ```
[260](https://docs.rs#260)//! # use mockall::*;
[261](https://docs.rs#261)//! # use mockall::predicate::*;
[262](https://docs.rs#262)//! #[automock]
[263](https://docs.rs#263)//! trait Foo {
[264](https://docs.rs#264)//!     fn open(&self, path: String) -> Option<u32>;
[265](https://docs.rs#265)//! }
[266](https://docs.rs#266)//!
[267](https://docs.rs#267)//! let mut mock = MockFoo::new();
[268](https://docs.rs#268)//! mock.expect_open()
[269](https://docs.rs#269)//!     .with(eq(String::from("something.txt")))
[270](https://docs.rs#270)//!     .returning(|_| Some(5));
[271](https://docs.rs#271)//! mock.expect_open()
[272](https://docs.rs#272)//!     .return_const(None);
[273](https://docs.rs#273)//! ```
[274](https://docs.rs#274)//!
[275](https://docs.rs#275)//! ## Call counts
[276](https://docs.rs#276)//!
[277](https://docs.rs#277)//! By default, every expectation is allowed to be called an unlimited number of
[278](https://docs.rs#278)//! times.  But Mockall can optionally verify that an expectation was called a
[279](https://docs.rs#279)//! fixed number of times, or any number of times within a given range.
[280](https://docs.rs#280)//!
[281](https://docs.rs#281)//! ```should_panic
[282](https://docs.rs#282)//! # use mockall::*;
[283](https://docs.rs#283)//! # use mockall::predicate::*;
[284](https://docs.rs#284)//! #[automock]
[285](https://docs.rs#285)//! trait Foo {
[286](https://docs.rs#286)//!     fn foo(&self, x: u32);
[287](https://docs.rs#287)//! }
[288](https://docs.rs#288)//!
[289](https://docs.rs#289)//! let mut mock = MockFoo::new();
[290](https://docs.rs#290)//! mock.expect_foo()
[291](https://docs.rs#291)//!     .times(1)
[292](https://docs.rs#292)//!     .return_const(());
[293](https://docs.rs#293)//!
[294](https://docs.rs#294)//! mock.foo(0);    // Ok
[295](https://docs.rs#295)//! mock.foo(1);    // Panics!
[296](https://docs.rs#296)//! ```
[297](https://docs.rs#297)//!
[298](https://docs.rs#298)//! See also
[299](https://docs.rs#299)//! [`never`](examples::__mock_MockFoo_Foo::__foo::Expectation::never) and
[300](https://docs.rs#300)//! [`times`](examples::__mock_MockFoo_Foo::__foo::Expectation::times).
[301](https://docs.rs#301)//!
[302](https://docs.rs#302)//! ## Sequences
[303](https://docs.rs#303)//!
[304](https://docs.rs#304)//! By default expectations may be matched in any order.  But it's possible to
[305](https://docs.rs#305)//! specify the order by using a [`Sequence`].  Any expectations may be added to
[306](https://docs.rs#306)//! the same sequence.  They don't even need to come from the same object.
[307](https://docs.rs#307)//!
[308](https://docs.rs#308)//! ```should_panic
[309](https://docs.rs#309)//! # use mockall::*;
[310](https://docs.rs#310)//! #[automock]
[311](https://docs.rs#311)//! trait Foo {
[312](https://docs.rs#312)//!     fn foo(&self);
[313](https://docs.rs#313)//! }
[314](https://docs.rs#314)//!
[315](https://docs.rs#315)//! # fn main() {
[316](https://docs.rs#316)//! let mut seq = Sequence::new();
[317](https://docs.rs#317)//!
[318](https://docs.rs#318)//! let mut mock1 = MockFoo::new();
[319](https://docs.rs#319)//! mock1.expect_foo()
[320](https://docs.rs#320)//!     .times(1)
[321](https://docs.rs#321)//!     .in_sequence(&mut seq)
[322](https://docs.rs#322)//!     .returning(|| ());
[323](https://docs.rs#323)//!
[324](https://docs.rs#324)//! let mut mock2 = MockFoo::new();
[325](https://docs.rs#325)//! mock2.expect_foo()
[326](https://docs.rs#326)//!     .times(1)
[327](https://docs.rs#327)//!     .in_sequence(&mut seq)
[328](https://docs.rs#328)//!     .returning(|| ());
[329](https://docs.rs#329)//!
[330](https://docs.rs#330)//! mock2.foo();    // Panics!  mock1.foo should've been called first.
[331](https://docs.rs#331)//! # }
[332](https://docs.rs#332)//! ```
[333](https://docs.rs#333)//!
[334](https://docs.rs#334)//! ## Checkpoints
[335](https://docs.rs#335)//!
[336](https://docs.rs#336)//! Sometimes its useful to validate all expectations mid-test, throw them away,
[337](https://docs.rs#337)//! and add new ones.  That's what checkpoints do.  Every mock object has a
[338](https://docs.rs#338)//! `checkpoint` method.  When called, it will immediately validate all methods'
[339](https://docs.rs#339)//! expectations.  So any expectations that haven't satisfied their call count
[340](https://docs.rs#340)//! will panic.  Afterwards, those expectations will be cleared so you can add
[341](https://docs.rs#341)//! new expectations and keep testing.
[342](https://docs.rs#342)//!
[343](https://docs.rs#343)//! ```should_panic
[344](https://docs.rs#344)//! # use mockall::*;
[345](https://docs.rs#345)//! #[automock]
[346](https://docs.rs#346)//! trait Foo {
[347](https://docs.rs#347)//!     fn foo(&self);
[348](https://docs.rs#348)//! }
[349](https://docs.rs#349)//!
[350](https://docs.rs#350)//! let mut mock = MockFoo::new();
[351](https://docs.rs#351)//! mock.expect_foo()
[352](https://docs.rs#352)//!     .times(2)
[353](https://docs.rs#353)//!     .returning(|| ());
[354](https://docs.rs#354)//!
[355](https://docs.rs#355)//! mock.foo();
[356](https://docs.rs#356)//! mock.checkpoint();  // Panics!  foo hasn't yet been called twice.
[357](https://docs.rs#357)//! ```
[358](https://docs.rs#358)//!
[359](https://docs.rs#359)//! ```should_panic
[360](https://docs.rs#360)//! # use mockall::*;
[361](https://docs.rs#361)//! #[automock]
[362](https://docs.rs#362)//! trait Foo {
[363](https://docs.rs#363)//!     fn foo(&self);
[364](https://docs.rs#364)//! }
[365](https://docs.rs#365)//!
[366](https://docs.rs#366)//! # fn main() {
[367](https://docs.rs#367)//! let mut mock = MockFoo::new();
[368](https://docs.rs#368)//! mock.expect_foo()
[369](https://docs.rs#369)//!     .times(1)
[370](https://docs.rs#370)//!     .returning(|| ());
[371](https://docs.rs#371)//!
[372](https://docs.rs#372)//! mock.foo();
[373](https://docs.rs#373)//! mock.checkpoint();
[374](https://docs.rs#374)//! mock.foo();         // Panics!  The expectation has been cleared.
[375](https://docs.rs#375)//! # }
[376](https://docs.rs#376)//! ```
[377](https://docs.rs#377)//!
[378](https://docs.rs#378)//! ## Reference arguments
[379](https://docs.rs#379)//!
[380](https://docs.rs#380)//! Mockall can mock methods with reference arguments, too.  There's one catch:
[381](https://docs.rs#381)//! the matcher [`Predicate`] will take reference arguments by value, not by
[382](https://docs.rs#382)//! reference.
[383](https://docs.rs#383)//!
[384](https://docs.rs#384)//! ```
[385](https://docs.rs#385)//! # use mockall::*;
[386](https://docs.rs#386)//! #[automock]
[387](https://docs.rs#387)//! trait Foo {
[388](https://docs.rs#388)//!     fn foo(&self, x: &u32) -> u32;
[389](https://docs.rs#389)//! }
[390](https://docs.rs#390)//!
[391](https://docs.rs#391)//! let mut mock = MockFoo::new();
[392](https://docs.rs#392)//! let e = mock.expect_foo()
[393](https://docs.rs#393)//!     // Note that x is a &u32, not a &&u32
[394](https://docs.rs#394)//!     .withf(|x: &u32| *x == 5)
[395](https://docs.rs#395)//!     .returning(|x: &u32| *x + 1);
[396](https://docs.rs#396)//!
[397](https://docs.rs#397)//! assert_eq!(6, mock.foo(&5));
[398](https://docs.rs#398)//! ```
[399](https://docs.rs#399)//!
[400](https://docs.rs#400)//! ## Reference return values
[401](https://docs.rs#401)//!
[402](https://docs.rs#402)//! Mockall can also use reference return values.  There is one restriction: the
[403](https://docs.rs#403)//! lifetime of the returned reference must be either the same as the lifetime
[404](https://docs.rs#404)//! of the mock object, or `'static`.
[405](https://docs.rs#405)//!
[406](https://docs.rs#406)//! Mockall creates different expectation types for methods that return
[407](https://docs.rs#407)//! references.  Their API is the same as the basic `Expectation`, except for
[408](https://docs.rs#408)//! setting return values.
[409](https://docs.rs#409)//!
[410](https://docs.rs#410)//! Methods that return `'static` references work just like methods that return
[411](https://docs.rs#411)//! any other `'static` value.
[412](https://docs.rs#412)//! ```
[413](https://docs.rs#413)//! # use mockall::*;
[414](https://docs.rs#414)//! struct Thing(u32);
[415](https://docs.rs#415)//!
[416](https://docs.rs#416)//! #[automock]
[417](https://docs.rs#417)//! trait Container {
[418](https://docs.rs#418)//!     fn get(&self, i: u32) -> &'static Thing;
[419](https://docs.rs#419)//! }
[420](https://docs.rs#420)//!
[421](https://docs.rs#421)//! # fn main() {
[422](https://docs.rs#422)//! const THING: Thing = Thing(42);
[423](https://docs.rs#423)//! let mut mock = MockContainer::new();
[424](https://docs.rs#424)//! mock.expect_get()
[425](https://docs.rs#425)//!     .return_const(&THING);
[426](https://docs.rs#426)//!
[427](https://docs.rs#427)//! assert_eq!(42, mock.get(0).0);
[428](https://docs.rs#428)//! # }
[429](https://docs.rs#429)//! ```
[430](https://docs.rs#430)//!
[431](https://docs.rs#431)//! Methods that take a `&self` argument use an `Expectation` class like
[432](https://docs.rs#432)//! [this](examples::__mock_MockFoo_Foo::__bar::Expectation),
[433](https://docs.rs#433)//! which
[434](https://docs.rs#434)//! gets its return value from the
[435](https://docs.rs#435)//! [`return_const`](examples::__mock_MockFoo_Foo::__bar::Expectation::return_const) method.
[436](https://docs.rs#436)//!
[437](https://docs.rs#437)//! ```
[438](https://docs.rs#438)//! # use mockall::*;
[439](https://docs.rs#439)//! struct Thing(u32);
[440](https://docs.rs#440)//!
[441](https://docs.rs#441)//! #[automock]
[442](https://docs.rs#442)//! trait Container {
[443](https://docs.rs#443)//!     fn get(&self, i: u32) -> &Thing;
[444](https://docs.rs#444)//! }
[445](https://docs.rs#445)//!
[446](https://docs.rs#446)//! # fn main() {
[447](https://docs.rs#447)//! let thing = Thing(42);
[448](https://docs.rs#448)//! let mut mock = MockContainer::new();
[449](https://docs.rs#449)//! mock.expect_get()
[450](https://docs.rs#450)//!     .return_const(thing);
[451](https://docs.rs#451)//!
[452](https://docs.rs#452)//! assert_eq!(42, mock.get(0).0);
[453](https://docs.rs#453)//! # }
[454](https://docs.rs#454)//! ```
[455](https://docs.rs#455)//!
[456](https://docs.rs#456)//! Methods that take a `&mut self` argument use an `Expectation` class like
[457](https://docs.rs#457)//! [this](examples::__mock_MockFoo_Foo::__baz::Expectation),
[458](https://docs.rs#458)//! class, regardless of whether the return value is actually mutable.  They can
[459](https://docs.rs#459)//! take their return value either from the
[460](https://docs.rs#460)//! [`return_var`](examples::__mock_MockFoo_Foo::__baz::Expectation::return_var)
[461](https://docs.rs#461)//! or
[462](https://docs.rs#462)//! [`returning`](examples::__mock_MockFoo_Foo::__baz::Expectation::returning)
[463](https://docs.rs#463)//! methods.
[464](https://docs.rs#464)//!
[465](https://docs.rs#465)//! ```
[466](https://docs.rs#466)//! # use mockall::*;
[467](https://docs.rs#467)//! struct Thing(u32);
[468](https://docs.rs#468)//!
[469](https://docs.rs#469)//! #[automock]
[470](https://docs.rs#470)//! trait Container {
[471](https://docs.rs#471)//!     fn get_mut(&mut self, i: u32) -> &mut Thing;
[472](https://docs.rs#472)//! }
[473](https://docs.rs#473)//!
[474](https://docs.rs#474)//! # fn main() {
[475](https://docs.rs#475)//! let thing = Thing(42);
[476](https://docs.rs#476)//! let mut mock = MockContainer::new();
[477](https://docs.rs#477)//! mock.expect_get_mut()
[478](https://docs.rs#478)//!     .return_var(thing);
[479](https://docs.rs#479)//!
[480](https://docs.rs#480)//! mock.get_mut(0).0 = 43;
[481](https://docs.rs#481)//! assert_eq!(43, mock.get_mut(0).0);
[482](https://docs.rs#482)//! # }
[483](https://docs.rs#483)//! ```
[484](https://docs.rs#484)//!
[485](https://docs.rs#485)//! Unsized types that are common targets for
[486](https://docs.rs#486)//! [`Deref`](core::ops::Deref)
[487](https://docs.rs#487)//! are special.  Mockall
[488](https://docs.rs#488)//! will automatically use the type's owned form for the Expectation.
[489](https://docs.rs#489)//! Currently, the
[490](https://docs.rs#490)//! [`CStr`](std::ffi::CStr),
[491](https://docs.rs#491)//! [`OsStr`](std::ffi::OsStr),
[492](https://docs.rs#492)//! [`Path`](std::path::Path),
[493](https://docs.rs#493)//! [`Slice`][std::slice],
[494](https://docs.rs#494)//! and
[495](https://docs.rs#495)//! [`str`](std::str)
[496](https://docs.rs#496)//! types are supported.  Using this feature is automatic:
[497](https://docs.rs#497)//!
[498](https://docs.rs#498)//! ```
[499](https://docs.rs#499)//! # use mockall::*;
[500](https://docs.rs#500)//! #[automock]
[501](https://docs.rs#501)//! trait Foo {
[502](https://docs.rs#502)//!     fn name(&self) -> &str;
[503](https://docs.rs#503)//! }
[504](https://docs.rs#504)//!
[505](https://docs.rs#505)//! let mut mock = MockFoo::new();
[506](https://docs.rs#506)//! mock.expect_name().return_const("abcd".to_owned());
[507](https://docs.rs#507)//! assert_eq!("abcd", mock.name());
[508](https://docs.rs#508)//! ```
[509](https://docs.rs#509)//!
[510](https://docs.rs#510)//! Similarly, Mockall will use a Boxed trait object for the Expectation of
[511](https://docs.rs#511)//! methods that return references to trait objects.
[512](https://docs.rs#512)//!
[513](https://docs.rs#513)//! ```
[514](https://docs.rs#514)//! # use mockall::*;
[515](https://docs.rs#515)//! # use std::fmt::Display;
[516](https://docs.rs#516)//! #[automock]
[517](https://docs.rs#517)//! trait Foo {
[518](https://docs.rs#518)//!     fn name(&self) -> &dyn Display;
[519](https://docs.rs#519)//! }
[520](https://docs.rs#520)//!
[521](https://docs.rs#521)//! # fn main() {
[522](https://docs.rs#522)//! let mut mock = MockFoo::new();
[523](https://docs.rs#523)//! mock.expect_name().return_const(Box::new("abcd"));
[524](https://docs.rs#524)//! assert_eq!("abcd", format!("{}", mock.name()));
[525](https://docs.rs#525)//! # }
[526](https://docs.rs#526)//! ```
[527](https://docs.rs#527)//!
[528](https://docs.rs#528)//!
[529](https://docs.rs#529)//! ## Impl Trait
[530](https://docs.rs#530)//!
[531](https://docs.rs#531)//! Rust 1.26.0 introduced the `impl Trait` feature.  It allows functions to
[532](https://docs.rs#532)//! return concrete but unnamed types (and, less usefully, to take them as
[533](https://docs.rs#533)//! arguments).  It's *almost* the same as `Box<dyn Trait>` but without the
[534](https://docs.rs#534)//! extra allocation.  Mockall supports deriving mocks for methods that return
[535](https://docs.rs#535)//! `impl Trait`, with limitations.  When you derive the mock for such a method,
[536](https://docs.rs#536)//! Mockall internally transforms the Expectation's return type to `Box<dyn
[537](https://docs.rs#537)//! Trait>`, without changing the mock method's signature.  So you can use it
[538](https://docs.rs#538)//! like this:
[539](https://docs.rs#539)//!
[540](https://docs.rs#540)//! ```
[541](https://docs.rs#541)//! # use mockall::*;
[542](https://docs.rs#542)//! # use std::fmt::Debug;
[543](https://docs.rs#543)//! struct Foo {}
[544](https://docs.rs#544)//! #[automock]
[545](https://docs.rs#545)//! impl Foo {
[546](https://docs.rs#546)//!     fn foo(&self) -> impl Debug {
[547](https://docs.rs#547)//!         // ...
[548](https://docs.rs#548)//!         # 4
[549](https://docs.rs#549)//!     }
[550](https://docs.rs#550)//! }
[551](https://docs.rs#551)//!
[552](https://docs.rs#552)//! # fn main() {
[553](https://docs.rs#553)//! let mut mock = MockFoo::new();
[554](https://docs.rs#554)//! mock.expect_foo()
[555](https://docs.rs#555)//!     .returning(|| Box::new(String::from("Hello, World!")));
[556](https://docs.rs#556)//! println!("{:?}", mock.foo());
[557](https://docs.rs#557)//! # }
[558](https://docs.rs#558)//! ```
[559](https://docs.rs#559)//!
[560](https://docs.rs#560)//! However, `impl Trait` isn't *exactly* equivalent to `Box<dyn Trait>` but
[561](https://docs.rs#561)//! with fewer allocations.  There are some things the former can do but the
[562](https://docs.rs#562)//! latter can't.  For one thing, you can't build a trait object out of a
[563](https://docs.rs#563)//! `Sized` trait.  So this won't work:
[564](https://docs.rs#564)//!
[565](https://docs.rs#565)//! ```compile_fail
[566](https://docs.rs#566)//! # use mockall::*;
[567](https://docs.rs#567)//! struct Foo {}
[568](https://docs.rs#568)//! #[automock]
[569](https://docs.rs#569)//! impl Foo {
[570](https://docs.rs#570)//!     fn foo(&self) -> impl Clone {
[571](https://docs.rs#571)//!         // ...
[572](https://docs.rs#572)//!         # 4
[573](https://docs.rs#573)//!     }
[574](https://docs.rs#574)//! }
[575](https://docs.rs#575)//! ```
[576](https://docs.rs#576)//!
[577](https://docs.rs#577)//! Nor can you create a trait object that implements two or more non-auto
[578](https://docs.rs#578)//! types.  So this won't work either:
[579](https://docs.rs#579)//!
[580](https://docs.rs#580)//! ```compile_fail
[581](https://docs.rs#581)//! # use mockall::*;
[582](https://docs.rs#582)//! struct Foo {}
[583](https://docs.rs#583)//! #[automock]
[584](https://docs.rs#584)//! impl Foo {
[585](https://docs.rs#585)//!     fn foo(&self) -> impl Debug + Display {
[586](https://docs.rs#586)//!         // ...
[587](https://docs.rs#587)//!         # 4
[588](https://docs.rs#588)//!     }
[589](https://docs.rs#589)//! }
[590](https://docs.rs#590)//! ```
[591](https://docs.rs#591)//!
[592](https://docs.rs#592)//! For such cases, there is no magic bullet.  The best way to mock methods like
[593](https://docs.rs#593)//! those would be to refactor them to return named (but possibly opaque) types
[594](https://docs.rs#594)//! instead.
[595](https://docs.rs#595)//!
[596](https://docs.rs#596)//! See Also [`impl-trait-for-returning-complex-types-with-ease.html`](https://rust-lang-nursery.github.io/edition-guide/rust-2018/trait-system/impl-trait-for-returning-complex-types-with-ease)
[597](https://docs.rs#597)//!
[598](https://docs.rs#598)//! ### impl Future
[599](https://docs.rs#599)//!
[600](https://docs.rs#600)//! Rust 1.36.0 added the `Future` trait.  Unlike virtually every trait that
[601](https://docs.rs#601)//! preceeded it, `Box<dyn Future>` is mostly useless.  Instead, you usually
[602](https://docs.rs#602)//! need a `Pin<Box<dyn Future>>`.  So that's what Mockall will do when you mock
[603](https://docs.rs#603)//! a method returning `impl Future` or the related `impl Stream`.  Just
[604](https://docs.rs#604)//! remember to use `pin` in your expectations, like this:
[605](https://docs.rs#605)//!
[606](https://docs.rs#606)//! ```
[607](https://docs.rs#607)//! # use mockall::*;
[608](https://docs.rs#608)//! # use std::fmt::Debug;
[609](https://docs.rs#609)//! # use futures::{Future, future};
[610](https://docs.rs#610)//! struct Foo {}
[611](https://docs.rs#611)//! #[automock]
[612](https://docs.rs#612)//! impl Foo {
[613](https://docs.rs#613)//!     fn foo(&self) -> impl Future<Output=i32> {
[614](https://docs.rs#614)//!         // ...
[615](https://docs.rs#615)//!         # future::ready(42)
[616](https://docs.rs#616)//!     }
[617](https://docs.rs#617)//! }
[618](https://docs.rs#618)//!
[619](https://docs.rs#619)//! # fn main() {
[620](https://docs.rs#620)//! let mut mock = MockFoo::new();
[621](https://docs.rs#621)//! mock.expect_foo()
[622](https://docs.rs#622)//!     .returning(|| Box::pin(future::ready(42)));
[623](https://docs.rs#623)//! # }
[624](https://docs.rs#624)//! ```
[625](https://docs.rs#625)//!
[626](https://docs.rs#626)//! ## Mocking structs
[627](https://docs.rs#627)//!
[628](https://docs.rs#628)//! Mockall mocks structs as well as traits.  The problem here is a namespace
[629](https://docs.rs#629)//! problem: it's hard to supply the mock object to your code under test,
[630](https://docs.rs#630)//! because it has a different name.  The solution is to alter import paths
[631](https://docs.rs#631)//! during test.  The easiest way to do that is with the
[632](https://docs.rs#632)//! [`mockall_double`](https://docs.rs/mockall_double/latest) crate.
[633](https://docs.rs#633)//!
[634](https://docs.rs#634)//! [`#[automock]`](attr.automock.html)
[635](https://docs.rs#635)//! works for structs that have a single `impl` block:
[636](https://docs.rs#636)//! ```no_run
[637](https://docs.rs#637)//! use mockall_double::double;
[638](https://docs.rs#638)//! mod thing {
[639](https://docs.rs#639)//!     use mockall::automock;
[640](https://docs.rs#640)//!     pub struct Thing{}
[641](https://docs.rs#641)//!     #[automock]
[642](https://docs.rs#642)//!     impl Thing {
[643](https://docs.rs#643)//!         pub fn foo(&self) -> u32 {
[644](https://docs.rs#644)//!             // ...
[645](https://docs.rs#645)//!             # unimplemented!()
[646](https://docs.rs#646)//!         }
[647](https://docs.rs#647)//!     }
[648](https://docs.rs#648)//! }
[649](https://docs.rs#649)//!
[650](https://docs.rs#650)//! #[double]
[651](https://docs.rs#651)//! use thing::Thing;
[652](https://docs.rs#652)//!
[653](https://docs.rs#653)//! fn do_stuff(thing: &Thing) -> u32 {
[654](https://docs.rs#654)//!     thing.foo()
[655](https://docs.rs#655)//! }
[656](https://docs.rs#656)//!
[657](https://docs.rs#657)//! #[cfg(test)]
[658](https://docs.rs#658)//! mod t {
[659](https://docs.rs#659)//!     use super::*;
[660](https://docs.rs#660)//!
[661](https://docs.rs#661)//!     #[test]
[662](https://docs.rs#662)//!     fn test_foo() {
[663](https://docs.rs#663)//!         let mut mock = Thing::default();
[664](https://docs.rs#664)//!         mock.expect_foo().returning(|| 42);
[665](https://docs.rs#665)//!         do_stuff(&mock);
[666](https://docs.rs#666)//!     }
[667](https://docs.rs#667)//! }
[668](https://docs.rs#668)//! # fn main() {}
[669](https://docs.rs#669)//! ```
[670](https://docs.rs#670)//! For structs with more than one `impl` block or that have unsupported
[671](https://docs.rs#671)//! `#[derive(X)]` attributes, e.g. `Clone`, see [`mock!`] instead.
[672](https://docs.rs#672)//!
[673](https://docs.rs#673)//! ## Generic methods
[674](https://docs.rs#674)//!
[675](https://docs.rs#675)//! Mocking generic methods is possible, but the exact process depends on
[676](https://docs.rs#676)//! whether the parameters are `'static`, non-`'static`, or lifetimes.
[677](https://docs.rs#677)//!
[678](https://docs.rs#678)//! ### With static parameters
[679](https://docs.rs#679)//!
[680](https://docs.rs#680)//! With fully `'static` parameters, the mock method is generic and so is its
[681](https://docs.rs#681)//! expect_* method.  The expect_* method usually must be called with a
[682](https://docs.rs#682)//! turbofish.  Expectations set with different generic parameters operate
[683](https://docs.rs#683)//! completely independently of one another.
[684](https://docs.rs#684)//!
[685](https://docs.rs#685)//! ```
[686](https://docs.rs#686)//! # use mockall::*;
[687](https://docs.rs#687)//! #[automock]
[688](https://docs.rs#688)//! trait Foo {
[689](https://docs.rs#689)//!     fn foo<T: 'static>(&self, t: T) -> i32;
[690](https://docs.rs#690)//! }
[691](https://docs.rs#691)//!
[692](https://docs.rs#692)//! let mut mock = MockFoo::new();
[693](https://docs.rs#693)//! mock.expect_foo::<i16>()
[694](https://docs.rs#694)//!     .returning(|t| i32::from(t));
[695](https://docs.rs#695)//! mock.expect_foo::<i8>()
[696](https://docs.rs#696)//!     .returning(|t| -i32::from(t));
[697](https://docs.rs#697)//!
[698](https://docs.rs#698)//! assert_eq!(5, mock.foo(5i16));
[699](https://docs.rs#699)//! assert_eq!(-5, mock.foo(5i8));
[700](https://docs.rs#700)//! ```
[701](https://docs.rs#701)//!
[702](https://docs.rs#702)//! ### With non-`static` type parameters
[703](https://docs.rs#703)//!
[704](https://docs.rs#704)//! Mocking methods with non-`'static` type parameters is harder.  The way
[705](https://docs.rs#705)//! Mockall does it is by turning the generic parameters into trait objects
[706](https://docs.rs#706)//! before evaluating expectations.  This makes the expect_* method concrete,
[707](https://docs.rs#707)//! rather than generic.  It also comes with many restrictions.  See
[708](https://docs.rs#708)//! [`#[concretize]`](attr.concretize.html) for more details.
[709](https://docs.rs#709)//!
[710](https://docs.rs#710)//! ### With generic lifetimes
[711](https://docs.rs#711)//!
[712](https://docs.rs#712)//! A method with a lifetime parameter is technically a generic method, but
[713](https://docs.rs#713)//! Mockall treats it like a non-generic method that must work for all possible
[714](https://docs.rs#714)//! lifetimes.  Mocking such a method is similar to mocking a non-generic
[715](https://docs.rs#715)//! method, with a few additional restrictions.  One restriction is that you
[716](https://docs.rs#716)//! can't match calls with `with`, you must use `withf` instead.  Another is
[717](https://docs.rs#717)//! that the generic lifetime may not appear as part of the return type.
[718](https://docs.rs#718)//! Finally, no method may have both generic lifetime parameters *and* generic
[719](https://docs.rs#719)//! type parameters.
[720](https://docs.rs#720)//!
[721](https://docs.rs#721)//! ```
[722](https://docs.rs#722)//! # use mockall::*;
[723](https://docs.rs#723)//! struct X<'a>(&'a i32);
[724](https://docs.rs#724)//!
[725](https://docs.rs#725)//! #[automock]
[726](https://docs.rs#726)//! trait Foo {
[727](https://docs.rs#727)//!     fn foo<'a>(&self, x: X<'a>) -> i32;
[728](https://docs.rs#728)//! }
[729](https://docs.rs#729)//!
[730](https://docs.rs#730)//! # fn main() {
[731](https://docs.rs#731)//! let mut mock = MockFoo::new();
[732](https://docs.rs#732)//! mock.expect_foo()
[733](https://docs.rs#733)//!     .withf(|f| *f.0 == 5)
[734](https://docs.rs#734)//!     .return_const(42);
[735](https://docs.rs#735)//! let x = X(&5);
[736](https://docs.rs#736)//! assert_eq!(42, mock.foo(x));
[737](https://docs.rs#737)//! # }
[738](https://docs.rs#738)//! ```
[739](https://docs.rs#739)//!
[740](https://docs.rs#740)//! ## Generic traits and structs
[741](https://docs.rs#741)//!
[742](https://docs.rs#742)//! Mocking generic structs and generic traits is not a problem.  The mock
[743](https://docs.rs#743)//! struct will be generic, too.  As with generic methods, lifetime parameters
[744](https://docs.rs#744)//! are not allowed.  However, as long as the generic parameters are not used by
[745](https://docs.rs#745)//! any static methods, then the parameters need not be `'static'`.
[746](https://docs.rs#746)//!
[747](https://docs.rs#747)//! ```
[748](https://docs.rs#748)//! # use mockall::*;
[749](https://docs.rs#749)//! #[automock]
[750](https://docs.rs#750)//! trait Foo<T> {
[751](https://docs.rs#751)//!     fn foo(&self, t: T) -> i32;
[752](https://docs.rs#752)//! }
[753](https://docs.rs#753)//!
[754](https://docs.rs#754)//! # fn main() {
[755](https://docs.rs#755)//! let mut mock = MockFoo::<i16>::new();
[756](https://docs.rs#756)//! mock.expect_foo()
[757](https://docs.rs#757)//!     .returning(|t| i32::from(t));
[758](https://docs.rs#758)//! assert_eq!(5, mock.foo(5i16));
[759](https://docs.rs#759)//! # }
[760](https://docs.rs#760)//! ```
[761](https://docs.rs#761)//!
[762](https://docs.rs#762)//! ## Associated types
[763](https://docs.rs#763)//!
[764](https://docs.rs#764)//! Traits with associated types can be mocked too.  Unlike generic traits, the
[765](https://docs.rs#765)//! mock struct will not be generic.  Instead, you must specify the associated
[766](https://docs.rs#766)//! types when defining the mock struct.  They're specified as metaitems to the
[767](https://docs.rs#767)//! [`#[automock]`](attr.automock.html) attribute.
[768](https://docs.rs#768)//!
[769](https://docs.rs#769)//! ```
[770](https://docs.rs#770)//! # use mockall::*;
[771](https://docs.rs#771)//! #[automock(type Key=u16; type Value=i32;)]
[772](https://docs.rs#772)//! pub trait A {
[773](https://docs.rs#773)//!     type Key;
[774](https://docs.rs#774)//!     type Value;
[775](https://docs.rs#775)//!     fn foo(&self, k: Self::Key) -> Self::Value;
[776](https://docs.rs#776)//! }
[777](https://docs.rs#777)//!
[778](https://docs.rs#778)//! let mut mock = MockA::new();
[779](https://docs.rs#779)//! mock.expect_foo()
[780](https://docs.rs#780)//!     .returning(|x: u16| i32::from(x));
[781](https://docs.rs#781)//! assert_eq!(4, mock.foo(4));
[782](https://docs.rs#782)//! ```
[783](https://docs.rs#783)//!
[784](https://docs.rs#784)//! ## Multiple and inherited traits
[785](https://docs.rs#785)//!
[786](https://docs.rs#786)//! Creating a mock struct that implements multiple traits, whether inherited or
[787](https://docs.rs#787)//! not, requires using the [`mock!`] macro.  But once created,
[788](https://docs.rs#788)//! using it is just the same as using any other mock object:
[789](https://docs.rs#789)//!
[790](https://docs.rs#790)//! ```
[791](https://docs.rs#791)//! # use mockall::*;
[792](https://docs.rs#792)//! pub trait A {
[793](https://docs.rs#793)//!     fn foo(&self);
[794](https://docs.rs#794)//! }
[795](https://docs.rs#795)//!
[796](https://docs.rs#796)//! pub trait B: A {
[797](https://docs.rs#797)//!     fn bar(&self);
[798](https://docs.rs#798)//! }
[799](https://docs.rs#799)//!
[800](https://docs.rs#800)//! mock! {
[801](https://docs.rs#801)//!     // Structure to mock
[802](https://docs.rs#802)//!     C {}
[803](https://docs.rs#803)//!     // First trait to implement on C
[804](https://docs.rs#804)//!     impl A for C {
[805](https://docs.rs#805)//!         fn foo(&self);
[806](https://docs.rs#806)//!     }
[807](https://docs.rs#807)//!     // Second trait to implement on C
[808](https://docs.rs#808)//!     impl B for C {
[809](https://docs.rs#809)//!         fn bar(&self);
[810](https://docs.rs#810)//!     }
[811](https://docs.rs#811)//! }
[812](https://docs.rs#812)//! # fn main() {
[813](https://docs.rs#813)//! let mut mock = MockC::new();
[814](https://docs.rs#814)//! mock.expect_foo().returning(|| ());
[815](https://docs.rs#815)//! mock.expect_bar().returning(|| ());
[816](https://docs.rs#816)//! mock.foo();
[817](https://docs.rs#817)//! mock.bar();
[818](https://docs.rs#818)//! # }
[819](https://docs.rs#819)//! ```
[820](https://docs.rs#820)//!
[821](https://docs.rs#821)//! ## External traits
[822](https://docs.rs#822)//!
[823](https://docs.rs#823)//! Mockall can mock traits and structs defined in external crates that are
[824](https://docs.rs#824)//! beyond your control, but you must use [`mock!`] instead of
[825](https://docs.rs#825)//! [`#[automock]`](attr.automock.html).  Mock an external trait like this:
[826](https://docs.rs#826)//!
[827](https://docs.rs#827)//! ```
[828](https://docs.rs#828)//! # use mockall::*;
[829](https://docs.rs#829)//! mock! {
[830](https://docs.rs#830)//!     MyStruct {}     // Name of the mock struct, less the "Mock" prefix
[831](https://docs.rs#831)//!     impl Clone for MyStruct {   // specification of the trait to mock
[832](https://docs.rs#832)//!         fn clone(&self) -> Self;
[833](https://docs.rs#833)//!     }
[834](https://docs.rs#834)//! }
[835](https://docs.rs#835)//!
[836](https://docs.rs#836)//! # fn main() {
[837](https://docs.rs#837)//! let mut mock1 = MockMyStruct::new();
[838](https://docs.rs#838)//! let mock2 = MockMyStruct::new();
[839](https://docs.rs#839)//! mock1.expect_clone()
[840](https://docs.rs#840)//!     .return_once(move || mock2);
[841](https://docs.rs#841)//! let cloned = mock1.clone();
[842](https://docs.rs#842)//! # }
[843](https://docs.rs#843)//! ```
[844](https://docs.rs#844)//!
[845](https://docs.rs#845)//! ## Static methods
[846](https://docs.rs#846)//!
[847](https://docs.rs#847)//! Mockall can also mock static methods.  But be careful!  The expectations are
[848](https://docs.rs#848)//! global.  If you want to use a static method in multiple tests, you must
[849](https://docs.rs#849)//! provide your own synchronization. See the [`synchronization
[850](https://docs.rs#850)//! example`](https://github.com/asomers/mockall/blob/master/mockall/examples/synchronization.rs)
[851](https://docs.rs#851)//! for a basic implementation. For ordinary methods, expectations are
[852](https://docs.rs#852)//! set on the mock object.  But static methods don't have any mock object.
[853](https://docs.rs#853)//! Instead, you must create a `Context` object just to set their expectations.
[854](https://docs.rs#854)//!
[855](https://docs.rs#855)//! ```
[856](https://docs.rs#856)//! # use mockall::*;
[857](https://docs.rs#857)//! #[automock]
[858](https://docs.rs#858)//! pub trait A {
[859](https://docs.rs#859)//!     fn foo() -> u32;
[860](https://docs.rs#860)//! }
[861](https://docs.rs#861)//!
[862](https://docs.rs#862)//! let ctx = MockA::foo_context();
[863](https://docs.rs#863)//! ctx.expect().returning(|| 99);
[864](https://docs.rs#864)//! assert_eq!(99, MockA::foo());
[865](https://docs.rs#865)//! ```
[866](https://docs.rs#866)//!
[867](https://docs.rs#867)//! A common pattern is mocking a trait with a constructor method.  In this case,
[868](https://docs.rs#868)//! you can easily set the mock constructor method to return a mock object.
[869](https://docs.rs#869)//!
[870](https://docs.rs#870)//! ```
[871](https://docs.rs#871)//! # use mockall::*;
[872](https://docs.rs#872)//! struct Foo{}
[873](https://docs.rs#873)//! #[automock]
[874](https://docs.rs#874)//! impl Foo {
[875](https://docs.rs#875)//!     fn from_i32(x: i32) -> Self {
[876](https://docs.rs#876)//!         // ...
[877](https://docs.rs#877)//!         # unimplemented!()
[878](https://docs.rs#878)//!     }
[879](https://docs.rs#879)//!     fn foo(&self) -> i32 {
[880](https://docs.rs#880)//!         // ...
[881](https://docs.rs#881)//!         # unimplemented!()
[882](https://docs.rs#882)//!     }
[883](https://docs.rs#883)//! }
[884](https://docs.rs#884)//!
[885](https://docs.rs#885)//! # fn main() {
[886](https://docs.rs#886)//! let ctx = MockFoo::from_i32_context();
[887](https://docs.rs#887)//! ctx.expect()
[888](https://docs.rs#888)//!     .returning(|x| {
[889](https://docs.rs#889)//!         let mut mock = MockFoo::default();
[890](https://docs.rs#890)//!         mock.expect_foo()
[891](https://docs.rs#891)//!             .return_const(x);
[892](https://docs.rs#892)//!         mock
[893](https://docs.rs#893)//!     });
[894](https://docs.rs#894)//! let foo = MockFoo::from_i32(42);
[895](https://docs.rs#895)//! assert_eq!(42, foo.foo());
[896](https://docs.rs#896)//! # }
[897](https://docs.rs#897)//! ```
[898](https://docs.rs#898)//!
[899](https://docs.rs#899)//! ### Generic static methods
[900](https://docs.rs#900)//!
[901](https://docs.rs#901)//! Mocking static methods of generic structs or traits, whether or not the
[902](https://docs.rs#902)//! methods themselves are generic, should work seamlessly as long as the
[903](https://docs.rs#903)//! generic parameter is `'static`
[904](https://docs.rs#904)//!
[905](https://docs.rs#905)//! ```
[906](https://docs.rs#906)//! # use mockall::*;
[907](https://docs.rs#907)//! #[automock]
[908](https://docs.rs#908)//! trait Foo<T: 'static> {
[909](https://docs.rs#909)//!     fn new(t: T) -> MockFoo<T>;
[910](https://docs.rs#910)//! }
[911](https://docs.rs#911)//!
[912](https://docs.rs#912)//! # fn main() {
[913](https://docs.rs#913)//! let ctx = MockFoo::<u32>::new_context();
[914](https://docs.rs#914)//! ctx.expect()
[915](https://docs.rs#915)//!     .returning(|_| MockFoo::default());
[916](https://docs.rs#916)//! let mock = MockFoo::<u32>::new(42u32);
[917](https://docs.rs#917)//! # }
[918](https://docs.rs#918)//! ```
[919](https://docs.rs#919)//!
[920](https://docs.rs#920)//! ### Context checkpoints
[921](https://docs.rs#921)//!
[922](https://docs.rs#922)//! The context object cleans up all expectations when it leaves scope.  It also
[923](https://docs.rs#923)//! has a `checkpoint` method that functions just like a mock object's
[924](https://docs.rs#924)//! `checkpoint` method.
[925](https://docs.rs#925)//!
[926](https://docs.rs#926)//! ```should_panic
[927](https://docs.rs#927)//! # use mockall::*;
[928](https://docs.rs#928)//! #[automock]
[929](https://docs.rs#929)//! pub trait A {
[930](https://docs.rs#930)//!     fn foo() -> u32;
[931](https://docs.rs#931)//! }
[932](https://docs.rs#932)//!
[933](https://docs.rs#933)//! let ctx = MockA::foo_context();
[934](https://docs.rs#934)//! ctx.expect()
[935](https://docs.rs#935)//!     .times(1)
[936](https://docs.rs#936)//!     .returning(|| 99);
[937](https://docs.rs#937)//! ctx.checkpoint();   // Panics!
[938](https://docs.rs#938)//! ```
[939](https://docs.rs#939)//!
[940](https://docs.rs#940)//! A mock object's checkpoint method does *not* checkpoint static methods.
[941](https://docs.rs#941)//! This behavior is useful when using multiple mock objects at once.  For
[942](https://docs.rs#942)//! example:
[943](https://docs.rs#943)//!
[944](https://docs.rs#944)//! ```
[945](https://docs.rs#945)//! # use mockall::*;
[946](https://docs.rs#946)//! #[automock]
[947](https://docs.rs#947)//! pub trait A {
[948](https://docs.rs#948)//!     fn build() -> Self;
[949](https://docs.rs#949)//!     fn bar(&self) -> i32;
[950](https://docs.rs#950)//! }
[951](https://docs.rs#951)//!
[952](https://docs.rs#952)//! # fn main() {
[953](https://docs.rs#953)//! let ctx = MockA::build_context();
[954](https://docs.rs#954)//! ctx.expect()
[955](https://docs.rs#955)//!     .times(2)
[956](https://docs.rs#956)//!     .returning(|| MockA::default());
[957](https://docs.rs#957)//! let mut mock0 = MockA::build();
[958](https://docs.rs#958)//! mock0.expect_bar().return_const(4);
[959](https://docs.rs#959)//! mock0.bar();
[960](https://docs.rs#960)//! mock0.checkpoint();     // Does not checkpoint the build method
[961](https://docs.rs#961)//! let mock1 = MockA::build();
[962](https://docs.rs#962)//! # }
[963](https://docs.rs#963)//! ```
[964](https://docs.rs#964)//!
[965](https://docs.rs#965)//! One more thing: Mockall normally creates a zero-argument `new` method for
[966](https://docs.rs#966)//! every mock struct.  But it *won't* do that when mocking a struct that
[967](https://docs.rs#967)//! already has a method named `new`.  The `default` method will still be
[968](https://docs.rs#968)//! present.
[969](https://docs.rs#969)//!
[970](https://docs.rs#970)//! ## Modules
[971](https://docs.rs#971)//!
[972](https://docs.rs#972)//! In addition to mocking types, Mockall can also derive mocks for
[973](https://docs.rs#973)//! entire modules of Rust functions.  Mockall will generate a new module named
[974](https://docs.rs#974)//! "mock_xxx", if "xxx" is the original module's name.  You can also use
[975](https://docs.rs#975)//! `#[double]` to selectively import the mock module.
[976](https://docs.rs#976)//!
[977](https://docs.rs#977)//! Be careful!  Module functions are static and so have the same caveats as
[978](https://docs.rs#978)//! [static methods](#static-methods) described above.
[979](https://docs.rs#979)//!
[980](https://docs.rs#980)//! ```
[981](https://docs.rs#981)//! # use mockall::*;
[982](https://docs.rs#982)//! # use mockall_double::*;
[983](https://docs.rs#983)//! mod outer {
[984](https://docs.rs#984)//!     use mockall::automock;
[985](https://docs.rs#985)//!     #[automock()]
[986](https://docs.rs#986)//!     pub(super) mod inner {
[987](https://docs.rs#987)//!         pub fn bar(x: u32) -> i64 {
[988](https://docs.rs#988)//!             // ...
[989](https://docs.rs#989)//!             # 4
[990](https://docs.rs#990)//!         }
[991](https://docs.rs#991)//!     }
[992](https://docs.rs#992)//! }
[993](https://docs.rs#993)//!
[994](https://docs.rs#994)//! #[double]
[995](https://docs.rs#995)//! use outer::inner;
[996](https://docs.rs#996)//!
[997](https://docs.rs#997)//! #[cfg(test)]
[998](https://docs.rs#998)//! mod t {
[999](https://docs.rs#999)//!     use super::*;
[1000](https://docs.rs#1000)//!
[1001](https://docs.rs#1001)//!     #[test]
[1002](https://docs.rs#1002)//!     fn test_foo_bar() {
[1003](https://docs.rs#1003)//!         let ctx = inner::bar_context();
[1004](https://docs.rs#1004)//!         ctx.expect()
[1005](https://docs.rs#1005)//!             .returning(|x| i64::from(x + 1));
[1006](https://docs.rs#1006)//!         assert_eq!(5, inner::bar(4));
[1007](https://docs.rs#1007)//!     }
[1008](https://docs.rs#1008)//! }
[1009](https://docs.rs#1009)//! # fn main() {}
[1010](https://docs.rs#1010)//! ```
[1011](https://docs.rs#1011)//!
[1012](https://docs.rs#1012)//! ### Foreign functions
[1013](https://docs.rs#1013)//!
[1014](https://docs.rs#1014)//! One reason to mock modules is when working with foreign functions.  Modules
[1015](https://docs.rs#1015)//! may contain foreign functions, even though structs and traits may not.  Like
[1016](https://docs.rs#1016)//! static methods, the expectations are global.
[1017](https://docs.rs#1017)//!
[1018](https://docs.rs#1018)//! ```
[1019](https://docs.rs#1019)//! # use mockall_double::*;
[1020](https://docs.rs#1020)//! mod outer {
[1021](https://docs.rs#1021)//!     # use mockall::*;
[1022](https://docs.rs#1022)//!     #[automock]
[1023](https://docs.rs#1023)//!     pub mod ffi {
[1024](https://docs.rs#1024)//!         extern "C" {
[1025](https://docs.rs#1025)//!             pub fn foo(x: u32) -> i64;
[1026](https://docs.rs#1026)//!         }
[1027](https://docs.rs#1027)//!     }
[1028](https://docs.rs#1028)//! }
[1029](https://docs.rs#1029)//!
[1030](https://docs.rs#1030)//! #[double]
[1031](https://docs.rs#1031)//! use outer::ffi;
[1032](https://docs.rs#1032)//!
[1033](https://docs.rs#1033)//! fn do_stuff() -> i64 {
[1034](https://docs.rs#1034)//!     unsafe{ ffi::foo(42) }
[1035](https://docs.rs#1035)//! }
[1036](https://docs.rs#1036)//!
[1037](https://docs.rs#1037)//! #[cfg(test)]
[1038](https://docs.rs#1038)//! mod t {
[1039](https://docs.rs#1039)//!     use super::*;
[1040](https://docs.rs#1040)//!
[1041](https://docs.rs#1041)//!     #[test]
[1042](https://docs.rs#1042)//!     fn test_foo() {
[1043](https://docs.rs#1043)//!         let ctx = ffi::foo_context();
[1044](https://docs.rs#1044)//!         ctx.expect()
[1045](https://docs.rs#1045)//!             .returning(|x| i64::from(x + 1));
[1046](https://docs.rs#1046)//!         assert_eq!(43, do_stuff());
[1047](https://docs.rs#1047)//!     }
[1048](https://docs.rs#1048)//! }
[1049](https://docs.rs#1049)//! # fn main() {}
[1050](https://docs.rs#1050)//! ```
[1051](https://docs.rs#1051)//!
[1052](https://docs.rs#1052)//! ## Debug
[1053](https://docs.rs#1053)//!
[1054](https://docs.rs#1054)//! `#[automock]` will automatically generate `Debug` impls when mocking traits
[1055](https://docs.rs#1055)//! and struct impls.  `mock!` will too, if you add a `#[derive(Debug)]`, like
[1056](https://docs.rs#1056)//! this:
[1057](https://docs.rs#1057)//! ```no_run
[1058](https://docs.rs#1058)//! # use mockall::*;
[1059](https://docs.rs#1059)//! mock! {
[1060](https://docs.rs#1060)//!     #[derive(Debug)]
[1061](https://docs.rs#1061)//!     pub Foo {}
[1062](https://docs.rs#1062)//! }
[1063](https://docs.rs#1063)//! # fn main() {
[1064](https://docs.rs#1064)//! #     format!("{:?}", &MockFoo::default());
[1065](https://docs.rs#1065)//! # }
[1066](https://docs.rs#1066)//! ```
[1067](https://docs.rs#1067)//!
[1068](https://docs.rs#1068)//! ## Async Traits
[1069](https://docs.rs#1069)//!
[1070](https://docs.rs#1070)//! Partial support for async traits was introduced in the Rust language since
[1071](https://docs.rs#1071)//! 1.75.0.
[1072](https://docs.rs#1072)//! Mockall is compatible with them, as well as both
[1073](https://docs.rs#1073)//! [`async_trait`](https://docs.rs/async-trait/latest/async_trait/) and
[1074](https://docs.rs#1074)//! [`trait_variant`](https://docs.rs/trait-variant/latest/trait_variant/)
[1075](https://docs.rs#1075)//! crates, with two important limitations:
[1076](https://docs.rs#1076)//!
[1077](https://docs.rs#1077)//! * The `#[automock]` attribute must appear _before_ the crate's attribute.
[1078](https://docs.rs#1078)//!
[1079](https://docs.rs#1079)//! * The `#[async_trait]` and `#[trait_variant::make]` macros must be
[1080](https://docs.rs#1080)//! imported with their canonical names.
[1081](https://docs.rs#1081)//!
[1082](https://docs.rs#1082)//! ```
[1083](https://docs.rs#1083)//! # use async_trait::async_trait;
[1084](https://docs.rs#1084)//! # use mockall::*;
[1085](https://docs.rs#1085)//! // async_trait works with both #[automock]
[1086](https://docs.rs#1086)//! #[automock]
[1087](https://docs.rs#1087)//! #[async_trait]
[1088](https://docs.rs#1088)//! pub trait Foo {
[1089](https://docs.rs#1089)//!    async fn foo(&self) -> u32;
[1090](https://docs.rs#1090)//! }
[1091](https://docs.rs#1091)//! // and mock!
[1092](https://docs.rs#1092)//! mock! {
[1093](https://docs.rs#1093)//!     pub Bar {}
[1094](https://docs.rs#1094)//!     #[async_trait]
[1095](https://docs.rs#1095)//!     impl Foo for Bar {
[1096](https://docs.rs#1096)//!         async fn foo(&self) -> u32;
[1097](https://docs.rs#1097)//!     }
[1098](https://docs.rs#1098)//! }
[1099](https://docs.rs#1099)//! # fn main() {}
[1100](https://docs.rs#1100)//! ```
[1101](https://docs.rs#1101)//!
[1102](https://docs.rs#1102)//! ## Crate features
[1103](https://docs.rs#1103)//!
[1104](https://docs.rs#1104)//! Mockall has a **nightly** feature.  Currently this feature has two
[1105](https://docs.rs#1105)//! effects:
[1106](https://docs.rs#1106)//!
[1107](https://docs.rs#1107)//! * The compiler will produce better error messages.
[1108](https://docs.rs#1108)//!
[1109](https://docs.rs#1109)//! * Expectations for methods whose return type implements `Default` needn't
[1110](https://docs.rs#1110)//!   have their return values explicitly set.  Instead, they will automatically
[1111](https://docs.rs#1111)//!   return the default value.
[1112](https://docs.rs#1112)//!
[1113](https://docs.rs#1113)//! With **nightly** enabled, you can omit the return value like this:
[1114](https://docs.rs#1114)#![cfg_attr(feature = "nightly", doc = "```")]
[1115](https://docs.rs#1115)#![cfg_attr(not(feature = "nightly"), doc = "```should_panic")]
[1116](https://docs.rs#1116)//! # use mockall::*;
[1117](https://docs.rs#1117)//! #[automock]
[1118](https://docs.rs#1118)//! trait Foo {
[1119](https://docs.rs#1119)//!     fn foo(&self) -> Vec<u32>;
[1120](https://docs.rs#1120)//! }
[1121](https://docs.rs#1121)//!
[1122](https://docs.rs#1122)//! let mut mock = MockFoo::new();
[1123](https://docs.rs#1123)//! mock.expect_foo();
[1124](https://docs.rs#1124)//! assert!(mock.foo().is_empty());
[1125](https://docs.rs#1125)//! ```
[1126](https://docs.rs#1126)//!

[1179](https://docs.rs#1179)pub mod examples;
[1180](https://docs.rs#1180)
[1181](https://docs.rs#1181)/// Automatically generate mock types for structs and traits.
[1182](https://docs.rs#1182)///
[1183](https://docs.rs#1183)/// This is by far the easiest way to use Mockall.  It works on almost all
[1184](https://docs.rs#1184)/// traits, and almost all structs that have a single `impl` block.  In either
[1185](https://docs.rs#1185)/// case, it will generate a mock struct whose name is the name of the mocked
[1186](https://docs.rs#1186)/// struct/trait prepended with "Mock".  For each method of the original, the
[1187](https://docs.rs#1187)/// mock struct will have a method named `expect_whatever` that allows you to
[1188](https://docs.rs#1188)/// set expectations.  There will also be one `checkpoint` method that calls
[1189](https://docs.rs#1189)/// [`checkpoint`] for every single mocked method.
[1190](https://docs.rs#1190)///
[1191](https://docs.rs#1191)/// # Examples
[1192](https://docs.rs#1192)///
[1193](https://docs.rs#1193)/// The simplest use case is mocking a no-frills trait
[1194](https://docs.rs#1194)/// ```
[1195](https://docs.rs#1195)/// # use mockall_derive::*;
[1196](https://docs.rs#1196)/// #[automock]
[1197](https://docs.rs#1197)/// pub trait Foo {
[1198](https://docs.rs#1198)///     fn foo(&self, key: i16);
[1199](https://docs.rs#1199)/// }
[1200](https://docs.rs#1200)///
[1201](https://docs.rs#1201)/// let mock = MockFoo::new();
[1202](https://docs.rs#1202)/// ```
[1203](https://docs.rs#1203)///
[1204](https://docs.rs#1204)/// Mocking a structure:
[1205](https://docs.rs#1205)/// ```
[1206](https://docs.rs#1206)/// # use mockall_derive::*;
[1207](https://docs.rs#1207)/// struct Foo {}
[1208](https://docs.rs#1208)/// #[automock]
[1209](https://docs.rs#1209)/// impl Foo {
[1210](https://docs.rs#1210)///     fn foo(&self) -> u32 {
[1211](https://docs.rs#1211)///         // ...
[1212](https://docs.rs#1212)///         # unimplemented!()
[1213](https://docs.rs#1213)///     }
[1214](https://docs.rs#1214)/// }
[1215](https://docs.rs#1215)/// ```
[1216](https://docs.rs#1216)///
[1217](https://docs.rs#1217)/// You can also mock a trait impl on a struct:
[1218](https://docs.rs#1218)/// ```
[1219](https://docs.rs#1219)/// # use mockall_derive::*;
[1220](https://docs.rs#1220)/// pub trait Foo {
[1221](https://docs.rs#1221)///     fn foo(&self, key: i16);
[1222](https://docs.rs#1222)/// }
[1223](https://docs.rs#1223)/// struct Bar{}
[1224](https://docs.rs#1224)/// #[automock]
[1225](https://docs.rs#1225)/// impl Foo for Bar {
[1226](https://docs.rs#1226)///     fn foo(&self, key: i16){
[1227](https://docs.rs#1227)///         // ...
[1228](https://docs.rs#1228)///         # unimplemented!()
[1229](https://docs.rs#1229)///     }
[1230](https://docs.rs#1230)/// }
[1231](https://docs.rs#1231)///
[1232](https://docs.rs#1232)/// let mock = MockBar::new();
[1233](https://docs.rs#1233)/// ```
[1234](https://docs.rs#1234)///
[1235](https://docs.rs#1235)/// Mocking a trait variant with a different name requires adding a metaitem to the
[1236](https://docs.rs#1236)/// attribute in order to mock the variant instead of the original:
[1237](https://docs.rs#1237)/// ```
[1238](https://docs.rs#1238)/// # use mockall_derive::*;
[1239](https://docs.rs#1239)/// #[automock(target = Foo)]
[1240](https://docs.rs#1240)/// #[trait_variant::make(Foo: Send)]
[1241](https://docs.rs#1241)/// trait LocalFoo {
[1242](https://docs.rs#1242)///     fn foo(&self) -> u32;
[1243](https://docs.rs#1243)/// }
[1244](https://docs.rs#1244)/// ```
[1245](https://docs.rs#1245)/// The example above demonstrates using `target = Foo`, which will generate
[1246](https://docs.rs#1246)/// a `MockFoo` struct suitable for mocking the `Foo` variant.
[1247](https://docs.rs#1247)/// Without `target = Foo`, `#[automock]` would have generated `MockLocalFoo`.
[1248](https://docs.rs#1248)///
[1249](https://docs.rs#1249)/// Mocking a trait with associated types requires adding a metaitem to the
[1250](https://docs.rs#1250)/// attribute:
[1251](https://docs.rs#1251)/// ```
[1252](https://docs.rs#1252)/// # use mockall_derive::*;
[1253](https://docs.rs#1253)/// #[automock(type Item=u32;)]
[1254](https://docs.rs#1254)/// trait Foo {
[1255](https://docs.rs#1255)///     type Item;
[1256](https://docs.rs#1256)///     fn foo(&self) -> Self::Item;
[1257](https://docs.rs#1257)/// }
[1258](https://docs.rs#1258)/// ```
[1259](https://docs.rs#1259)///
[1260](https://docs.rs#1260)/// It can mock a module full of functions.  In this case, the mock functions
[1261](https://docs.rs#1261)/// will be found in a module whose name is prepended with `mock_`.
[1262](https://docs.rs#1262)///
[1263](https://docs.rs#1263)/// ```
[1264](https://docs.rs#1264)/// # use mockall_derive::*;
[1265](https://docs.rs#1265)/// #[automock]
[1266](https://docs.rs#1266)/// mod mymod {
[1267](https://docs.rs#1267)///     pub fn foo() -> u32 {
[1268](https://docs.rs#1268)///        // ...
[1269](https://docs.rs#1269)///        # unimplemented!()
[1270](https://docs.rs#1270)///     }
[1271](https://docs.rs#1271)/// }
[1272](https://docs.rs#1272)/// ```
[1273](https://docs.rs#1273)/// Finally, `#[automock]` can also mock foreign functions.  This works just
[1274](https://docs.rs#1274)/// like mocking a module.
[1275](https://docs.rs#1275)///
[1276](https://docs.rs#1276)/// ```
[1277](https://docs.rs#1277)/// # use mockall_derive::*;
[1278](https://docs.rs#1278)/// #[automock]
[1279](https://docs.rs#1279)/// mod ffi {
[1280](https://docs.rs#1280)///     extern "C" {
[1281](https://docs.rs#1281)///         pub fn foo() -> u32;
[1282](https://docs.rs#1282)///     }
[1283](https://docs.rs#1283)/// }
[1284](https://docs.rs#1284)/// ```
[1285](https://docs.rs#1285)///
[1286](https://docs.rs#1286)/// [`checkpoint`]: ../mockall/index.html#checkpoints
[1287](https://docs.rs#1287)///
[1288](https://docs.rs#1288)/// # Limitations
[1289](https://docs.rs#1289)///
[1290](https://docs.rs#1290)/// `#[automock]` can't handle everything.  There are some cases where
[1291](https://docs.rs#1291)/// you will need to use [`mock!`] instead:
[1292](https://docs.rs#1292)/// * Mocking a struct that has multiple `impl` blocks, including
[1293](https://docs.rs#1293)///   structs that implement traits.
[1294](https://docs.rs#1294)/// * Mocking a struct or trait defined in another crate.
[1295](https://docs.rs#1295)/// * Mocking a trait with trait bounds.
[1296](https://docs.rs#1296)/// * If the autogenerated "MockFoo" name isn't acceptable, and you want
[1297](https://docs.rs#1297)///   to choose your own name for the mock structure.
[1298](https://docs.rs#1298)pub use mockall_derive::automock;
[1299](https://docs.rs#1299)
[1300](https://docs.rs#1300)/// Decorates a method or function to tell Mockall to treat its generic arguments
[1301](https://docs.rs#1301)/// as trait objects when creating expectations.
[1302](https://docs.rs#1302)///
[1303](https://docs.rs#1303)/// This allows users to use non-`'static` generic parameters, which otherwise
[1304](https://docs.rs#1304)/// can't be mocked.  The downsides of using this attribute are:
[1305](https://docs.rs#1305)///
[1306](https://docs.rs#1306)/// * Mockall can't tell if a parameter isn't `'static`, so you must annotate
[1307](https://docs.rs#1307)///   such methods with the `#[mockall::concretize]` attribute.
[1308](https://docs.rs#1308)/// * Generic methods will share expectations for all argument types.  That is,
[1309](https://docs.rs#1309)///   you won't be able to do `my_mock.expect_foo::<i32>(...)`.
[1310](https://docs.rs#1310)/// * It can't be used on methods with a closure argument (though this may be
[1311](https://docs.rs#1311)///   fixable).
[1312](https://docs.rs#1312)/// * Concretized methods' expectations may only be matched with `.withf` or
[1313](https://docs.rs#1313)///   `.withf_st`, not `.with`.
[1314](https://docs.rs#1314)/// * It only works for parameters that can be turned into a trait object.
[1315](https://docs.rs#1315)///   (may be fixable).
[1316](https://docs.rs#1316)/// * Mockall needs to know how to turn the function argument into a trait
[1317](https://docs.rs#1317)///   object.  Given a generic parameter `T`, currently supported patterns are:
[1318](https://docs.rs#1318)///   - `T`
[1319](https://docs.rs#1319)///   - `&T`
[1320](https://docs.rs#1320)///   - `&mut T`
[1321](https://docs.rs#1321)///   - `&[T]`
[1322](https://docs.rs#1322)///
[1323](https://docs.rs#1323)/// # Examples
[1324](https://docs.rs#1324)/// ```
[1325](https://docs.rs#1325)/// # use std::path::Path;
[1326](https://docs.rs#1326)/// # use mockall::{automock, concretize};
[1327](https://docs.rs#1327)/// #[automock]
[1328](https://docs.rs#1328)/// trait Foo {
[1329](https://docs.rs#1329)///     #[mockall::concretize]
[1330](https://docs.rs#1330)///     fn foo<P: AsRef<Path>>(&self, p: P);
[1331](https://docs.rs#1331)/// }
[1332](https://docs.rs#1332)///
[1333](https://docs.rs#1333)/// # fn main() {
[1334](https://docs.rs#1334)/// let mut mock = MockFoo::new();
[1335](https://docs.rs#1335)/// mock.expect_foo()
[1336](https://docs.rs#1336)///     .withf(|p| p.as_ref() == Path::new("/tmp"))
[1337](https://docs.rs#1337)///     .return_const(());
[1338](https://docs.rs#1338)/// mock.foo(Path::new("/tmp"));
[1339](https://docs.rs#1339)/// # }
[1340](https://docs.rs#1340)/// ```
[1341](https://docs.rs#1341)///
[1342](https://docs.rs#1342)/// NB: This attribute must be imported with its canonical name.  It won't work
[1343](https://docs.rs#1343)/// otherwise!
[1344](https://docs.rs#1344)/// ```compile_fail
[1345](https://docs.rs#1345)/// use mockall::concretize as something_else;
[1346](https://docs.rs#1346)/// #[mockall::automock]
[1347](https://docs.rs#1347)/// trait Foo {
[1348](https://docs.rs#1348)///     #[something_else]
[1349](https://docs.rs#1349)///     fn foo<T>(&self, t: T);
[1350](https://docs.rs#1350)/// }
[1351](https://docs.rs#1351)/// ```
[1352](https://docs.rs#1352)pub use mockall_derive::concretize;
[1353](https://docs.rs#1353)
[1354](https://docs.rs#1354)/// Manually mock a structure.
[1355](https://docs.rs#1355)///
[1356](https://docs.rs#1356)/// Sometimes [`automock`] can't be used.  In those cases you can use `mock!`,
[1357](https://docs.rs#1357)/// which basically involves repeating the struct's or trait's definitions.
[1358](https://docs.rs#1358)///
[1359](https://docs.rs#1359)/// The format is:
[1360](https://docs.rs#1360)///
[1361](https://docs.rs#1361)/// * Optional visibility specifier
[1362](https://docs.rs#1362)/// * Real structure name and generics fields
[1363](https://docs.rs#1363)/// * 0 or more methods of the structure, written without bodies, enclosed in a
[1364](https://docs.rs#1364)///   {} block
[1365](https://docs.rs#1365)/// * 0 or more impl blocks implementing traits on the structure, also without
[1366](https://docs.rs#1366)///   bodies.
[1367](https://docs.rs#1367)///
[1368](https://docs.rs#1368)/// # Examples
[1369](https://docs.rs#1369)///
[1370](https://docs.rs#1370)/// Mock a trait.  This is the simplest use case.
[1371](https://docs.rs#1371)/// ```
[1372](https://docs.rs#1372)/// # use mockall_derive::mock;
[1373](https://docs.rs#1373)/// trait Foo {
[1374](https://docs.rs#1374)///     fn foo(&self, x: u32);
[1375](https://docs.rs#1375)/// }
[1376](https://docs.rs#1376)/// mock!{
[1377](https://docs.rs#1377)///     pub MyStruct<T: Clone + 'static> {
[1378](https://docs.rs#1378)///         fn bar(&self) -> u8;
[1379](https://docs.rs#1379)///     }
[1380](https://docs.rs#1380)///     impl<T: Clone + 'static> Foo for MyStruct<T> {
[1381](https://docs.rs#1381)///         fn foo(&self, x: u32);
[1382](https://docs.rs#1382)///     }
[1383](https://docs.rs#1383)/// }
[1384](https://docs.rs#1384)/// # fn main() {}
[1385](https://docs.rs#1385)/// ```
[1386](https://docs.rs#1386)/// Mocking an unsupported `#[derive(X)]` attribute, e.g. [`Clone`], is
[1387](https://docs.rs#1387)/// similar.
[1388](https://docs.rs#1388)/// ```
[1389](https://docs.rs#1389)/// # use mockall_derive::mock;
[1390](https://docs.rs#1390)/// #[derive(Clone)]
[1391](https://docs.rs#1391)/// struct MyStruct;
[1392](https://docs.rs#1392)///
[1393](https://docs.rs#1393)/// mock!{
[1394](https://docs.rs#1394)///     pub MyStruct {
[1395](https://docs.rs#1395)///         fn bar(&self);
[1396](https://docs.rs#1396)///     }
[1397](https://docs.rs#1397)///     impl Clone for MyStruct {
[1398](https://docs.rs#1398)///         fn clone(&self) -> Self;
[1399](https://docs.rs#1399)///     }
[1400](https://docs.rs#1400)/// }
[1401](https://docs.rs#1401)/// # fn main() {}
[1402](https://docs.rs#1402)/// ```
[1403](https://docs.rs#1403)///
[1404](https://docs.rs#1404)/// When mocking a generic struct's implementation of a generic trait, use the
[1405](https://docs.rs#1405)/// same name for their generic parameters.  For example, if you wanted to mock
[1406](https://docs.rs#1406)/// `Rc`, do
[1407](https://docs.rs#1407)/// ```
[1408](https://docs.rs#1408)/// # use mockall_derive::mock;
[1409](https://docs.rs#1409)/// mock!{
[1410](https://docs.rs#1410)///     pub Rc<T> {}
[1411](https://docs.rs#1411)///     impl<T> AsRef<T> for Rc<T> {
[1412](https://docs.rs#1412)///         fn as_ref(&self) -> &T;
[1413](https://docs.rs#1413)///     }
[1414](https://docs.rs#1414)/// }
[1415](https://docs.rs#1415)/// # fn main() {}
[1416](https://docs.rs#1416)/// ```
[1417](https://docs.rs#1417)/// *not*
[1418](https://docs.rs#1418)/// ```compile_fail
[1419](https://docs.rs#1419)/// # use mockall_derive::mock;
[1420](https://docs.rs#1420)/// mock!{
[1421](https://docs.rs#1421)///     pub Rc<Q> {}
[1422](https://docs.rs#1422)///     impl<T> AsRef<T> for Rc<T> {
[1423](https://docs.rs#1423)///         fn as_ref(&self) -> &T;
[1424](https://docs.rs#1424)///     }
[1425](https://docs.rs#1425)/// }
[1426](https://docs.rs#1426)/// # fn main() {}
[1427](https://docs.rs#1427)/// ```
[1428](https://docs.rs#1428)/// Associated types can easily be mocked by specifying a concrete type in the
[1429](https://docs.rs#1429)/// `mock!{}` invocation.
[1430](https://docs.rs#1430)/// ```
[1431](https://docs.rs#1431)/// # use mockall_derive::mock;
[1432](https://docs.rs#1432)/// mock!{
[1433](https://docs.rs#1433)///     MyIter {}
[1434](https://docs.rs#1434)///     impl Iterator for MyIter {
[1435](https://docs.rs#1435)///         type Item=u32;
[1436](https://docs.rs#1436)///
[1437](https://docs.rs#1437)///         fn next(&mut self) -> Option<<Self as Iterator>::Item>;
[1438](https://docs.rs#1438)///     }
[1439](https://docs.rs#1439)/// }
[1440](https://docs.rs#1440)/// # fn main() {}
[1441](https://docs.rs#1441)/// ```
[1442](https://docs.rs#1442)pub use mockall_derive::mock;
[1443](https://docs.rs#1443)
