[1593](https://docs.rs#1593)#[doc(hidden)]
[1594](https://docs.rs#1594)pub struct Times{
[1595](https://docs.rs#1595)    /// How many times has the expectation already been called?
[1596](https://docs.rs#1596)    count: AtomicUsize,
[1597](https://docs.rs#1597)    range: TimesRange
[1598](https://docs.rs#1598)}
[1599](https://docs.rs#1599)
[1600](https://docs.rs#1600)#[doc(hidden)]
[1601](https://docs.rs#1601)impl Times {
[1602](https://docs.rs#1602)    pub fn call(&self) -> Result<(), String> {
[1603](https://docs.rs#1603)        let count = self.count.fetch_add(1, Ordering::Relaxed) + 1;
[1604](https://docs.rs#1604)        if count >= self.range.0.end {
[1605](https://docs.rs#1605)            if self.range.0.end == 1 {
[1606](https://docs.rs#1606)                Err("should not have been called".to_owned())
[1607](https://docs.rs#1607)            } else {
[1608](https://docs.rs#1608)                Err(format!(
[1609](https://docs.rs#1609)                    "called {} times which is more than the expected {}",
[1610](https://docs.rs#1610)                    count,
[1611](https://docs.rs#1611)                    self.range.0.end - 1
[1612](https://docs.rs#1612)                ))
[1613](https://docs.rs#1613)            }
[1614](https://docs.rs#1614)        } else {
[1615](https://docs.rs#1615)            Ok(())
[1616](https://docs.rs#1616)        }
[1617](https://docs.rs#1617)    }
[1618](https://docs.rs#1618)
[1619](https://docs.rs#1619)    pub fn any(&mut self) {
[1620](https://docs.rs#1620)        self.range.0 = 0..usize::MAX;
[1621](https://docs.rs#1621)    }
[1622](https://docs.rs#1622)
[1623](https://docs.rs#1623)    /// Return how many times this expectation has been called
[1624](https://docs.rs#1624)    pub fn count(&self) -> usize {
[1625](https://docs.rs#1625)        self.count.load(Ordering::Relaxed)
[1626](https://docs.rs#1626)    }
[1627](https://docs.rs#1627)
[1628](https://docs.rs#1628)    /// Has this expectation already been called the maximum allowed number of
[1629](https://docs.rs#1629)    /// times?
[1630](https://docs.rs#1630)    pub fn is_done(&self) -> bool {
[1631](https://docs.rs#1631)        self.count.load(Ordering::Relaxed) >= self.range.0.end - 1
[1632](https://docs.rs#1632)    }
[1633](https://docs.rs#1633)
[1634](https://docs.rs#1634)    /// Is it required that this expectation be called an exact number of times,
[1635](https://docs.rs#1635)    /// or may it be satisfied by a range of call counts?
[1636](https://docs.rs#1636)    pub fn is_exact(&self) -> bool {
[1637](https://docs.rs#1637)        (self.range.0.end - self.range.0.start) == 1
[1638](https://docs.rs#1638)    }
[1639](https://docs.rs#1639)
[1640](https://docs.rs#1640)    /// Has this expectation already been called the expected number of times?
[1641](https://docs.rs#1641)    /// If not, was it too many or too few?
[1642](https://docs.rs#1642)    pub fn is_satisfied(&self) -> ExpectedCalls {
[1643](https://docs.rs#1643)        let satisfied_lower_bound = self.count.load(Ordering::Relaxed) >= self.range.0.start;
[1644](https://docs.rs#1644)        let satisfied_upper_bound = self.count.load(Ordering::Relaxed) < self.range.0.end;
[1645](https://docs.rs#1645)        if satisfied_lower_bound && satisfied_upper_bound {
[1646](https://docs.rs#1646)            ExpectedCalls::Satisfied
[1647](https://docs.rs#1647)        } else if satisfied_lower_bound {
[1648](https://docs.rs#1648)            ExpectedCalls::TooMany
[1649](https://docs.rs#1649)        } else {
[1650](https://docs.rs#1650)            ExpectedCalls::TooFew
[1651](https://docs.rs#1651)        }
[1652](https://docs.rs#1652)    }
[1653](https://docs.rs#1653)
[1654](https://docs.rs#1654)    /// The maximum number of times that this expectation must be called
[1655](https://docs.rs#1655)    pub fn maximum(&self) -> usize {
[1656](https://docs.rs#1656)        self.range.0.end - 1
[1657](https://docs.rs#1657)    }
[1658](https://docs.rs#1658)
[1659](https://docs.rs#1659)    /// The minimum number of times that this expectation must be called
[1660](https://docs.rs#1660)    pub fn minimum(&self) -> usize {
[1661](https://docs.rs#1661)        self.range.0.start
[1662](https://docs.rs#1662)    }
[1663](https://docs.rs#1663)

[1695](https://docs.rs#1695)
[1696](https://docs.rs#1696)/// Associates each `Expectation` with its place(s) in a [`Sequence`].
[1697](https://docs.rs#1697)///
[1698](https://docs.rs#1698)/// A SeqHandle is implicitly in one of five states, depending on the
[1699](https://docs.rs#1699)/// `satisfaction_level` within SeqInner:
[1700](https://docs.rs#1700)///
[1701](https://docs.rs#1701)/// 1. *Uncallable*
[1702](https://docs.rs#1702)///
[1703](https://docs.rs#1703)///     If a SeqHandle is in this state, other elements earlier in the sequence
[1704](https://docs.rs#1704)///     need to be satisfied first - i.e. by being called a minimum amount of
[1705](https://docs.rs#1705)///     times.
[1706](https://docs.rs#1706)///
[1707](https://docs.rs#1707)///     A SeqHandle is in this state if `satisfaction_level` is less than
[1708](https://docs.rs#1708)///     `min_seq`.
[1709](https://docs.rs#1709)///
[1710](https://docs.rs#1710)/// 2. *Callable*
[1711](https://docs.rs#1711)///
[1712](https://docs.rs#1712)///     Preceding expectation(s) are satisified, and we can progress to the
[1713](https://docs.rs#1713)///     current expectation, but preceding expectations may still be called
[1714](https://docs.rs#1714)///     further.
[1715](https://docs.rs#1715)///
[1716](https://docs.rs#1716)///     A SeqHandle is in this state if `satisfaction_level` is greater than
[1717](https://docs.rs#1717)///     or equal to `min_seq`, but less than `seq`.
[1718](https://docs.rs#1718)///
[1719](https://docs.rs#1719)/// 3. *Called*
[1720](https://docs.rs#1720)///
[1721](https://docs.rs#1721)///     The method has been called, and preceding expectations may no longer be
[1722](https://docs.rs#1722)///     called. Doing so would constitute an sequence ordering violation.
[1723](https://docs.rs#1723)///     However, the current count has not been satisfied yet, and the next
[1724](https://docs.rs#1724)///     element in sequence is not allowed to be called.
[1725](https://docs.rs#1725)///
[1726](https://docs.rs#1726)///     A SeqHandle is in this state if `satisfaction_level` is equal to `seq`
[1727](https://docs.rs#1727)///     and `has_called_state` is true.
[1728](https://docs.rs#1728)///
[1729](https://docs.rs#1729)///     If this state exists `min_seq` corresponding to the next expectation
[1730](https://docs.rs#1730)///
[1731](https://docs.rs#1731)/// 4. *Satisfied*
[1732](https://docs.rs#1732)///
[1733](https://docs.rs#1733)///     This element in the sequence has had its lower bound satisfied, and the
[1734](https://docs.rs#1734)///     next element in sequence is allowed to be called.
[1735](https://docs.rs#1735)///
[1736](https://docs.rs#1736)///     A SeqHandle is in this state if `satisfaction_level` is equal to `seq`
[1737](https://docs.rs#1737)///     if `has_called_state` is false, or equal to `seq + 1` if
[1738](https://docs.rs#1738)///     `has_called_state` is true.
[1739](https://docs.rs#1739)///     If the call count is zero, a SeqHandle is also satisfied once it is
[1740](https://docs.rs#1740)///     callable.
[1741](https://docs.rs#1741)///
[1742](https://docs.rs#1742)///     There is no `is_satisfied` method as the `min_seq` of the next
[1743](https://docs.rs#1743)///     expectation(s) are used to check whether this SeqHandle is in the
[1744](https://docs.rs#1744)///     satisfied state.
[1745](https://docs.rs#1745)///
[1746](https://docs.rs#1746)/// 5. *History*
[1747](https://docs.rs#1747)///
[1748](https://docs.rs#1748)///     This element can no longer be called, as succeeding elements have been
[1749](https://docs.rs#1749)///     performed in the sequence. If a handle is in the history state it can no
[1750](https://docs.rs#1750)///     longer be called, and will no longer be called.
[1751](https://docs.rs#1751)///
[1752](https://docs.rs#1752)///     A SeqHandle is in this state if `satisfaction_level` is greater than
[1753](https://docs.rs#1753)///     `seq`, or `seq + 1` if `has_called_state` is true.
[1754](https://docs.rs#1754)///
[1755](https://docs.rs#1755)#[doc(hidden)]
[1756](https://docs.rs#1756)pub struct SeqHandle {
[1757](https://docs.rs#1757)    inner: Arc<SeqInner>,
[1758](https://docs.rs#1758)    /// An ID counter for every `SeqHandle` associated with the same
[1759](https://docs.rs#1759)    /// [`Sequence`].  Starts at 0 and counts upwards.
[1760](https://docs.rs#1760)    ///
[1761](https://docs.rs#1761)    /// Identifies the `satisfaction_level` at which the corresponding
[1762](https://docs.rs#1762)    /// expectation may still be used, but preceding elements may not.
[1763](https://docs.rs#1763)    ///
[1764](https://docs.rs#1764)    /// If `has_called_state` is true, `satisfaction_level = seq` identifies
[1765](https://docs.rs#1765)    /// the state in which the expectation has been called, while `seq + 1`
[1766](https://docs.rs#1766)    /// identifies the state in which this expectation is satisfied.
[1767](https://docs.rs#1767)    seq: usize,
[1768](https://docs.rs#1768)    /// The minimum value the ID must have before the corresponding
[1769](https://docs.rs#1769)    /// `Expectation` may be called.
[1770](https://docs.rs#1770)    ///
[1771](https://docs.rs#1771)    /// Within a sequence `min_seq` is used to identify states where preceding
[1772](https://docs.rs#1772)    /// expectations are satisfied, and is kept constant if a expectation is
[1773](https://docs.rs#1773)    /// always satisfied, i.e., requires zero calls, allowing such expectations
[1774](https://docs.rs#1774)    /// to be skipped.
[1775](https://docs.rs#1775)    min_seq: usize,
[1776](https://docs.rs#1776)    /// Whether this `SeqHandle` differentiates between being called and
[1777](https://docs.rs#1777)    /// satisfied. A call count of Zero is already satisfied, and
[1778](https://docs.rs#1778)    /// state 3, Called, is always skipped. Similarly, once called, expecations
[1779](https://docs.rs#1779)    /// with a minimum call count of one are also satisfied.
[1780](https://docs.rs#1780)    ///
[1781](https://docs.rs#1781)    /// This flag is is also used to destinguish between state 2, Callable, and
[1782](https://docs.rs#1782)    /// state 4, Satisfied, in the case of the first expectation having a
[1783](https://docs.rs#1783)    /// minimum call count of one, as this expectation is not satisfied at
[1784](https://docs.rs#1784)    /// initialization.
[1785](https://docs.rs#1785)    has_called_state: bool,
[1786](https://docs.rs#1786)}
[1787](https://docs.rs#1787)
[1788](https://docs.rs#1788)impl SeqHandle {
[1789](https://docs.rs#1789)    /// Tell the Sequence that this expectation has been used.
[1790](https://docs.rs#1790)    pub fn called(&self) {
[1791](https://docs.rs#1791)        self.inner.called(self.seq, self.min_seq, self.has_called_state);
[1792](https://docs.rs#1792)    }
[1793](https://docs.rs#1793)
[1794](https://docs.rs#1794)    /// Tell the Sequence that this expectation has been fully satisfied
[1795](https://docs.rs#1795)    pub fn satisfy(&self) {
[1796](https://docs.rs#1796)        self.inner.satisfy(self.seq, self.min_seq, self.has_called_state);
[1797](https://docs.rs#1797)    }
[1798](https://docs.rs#1798)
[1799](https://docs.rs#1799)    /// Verify that this handle was called in the correct order
[1800](https://docs.rs#1800)    pub fn verify<F: Fn() -> String>(&self, desc: F) {
[1801](https://docs.rs#1801)        self.inner.verify(self.seq, self.min_seq, self.has_called_state, desc);
[1802](https://docs.rs#1802)    }
[1803](https://docs.rs#1803)
[1804](https://docs.rs#1804)    /// Check whether the current handle is part of history (i.e. has been
[1805](https://docs.rs#1805)    /// skipped or has already taken place)
[1806](https://docs.rs#1806)    pub fn is_history(&self) -> bool {
[1807](https://docs.rs#1807)        self.inner.is_history(self.seq, self.has_called_state)
[1808](https://docs.rs#1808)    }
[1809](https://docs.rs#1809)}
[1810](https://docs.rs#1810)
[1811](https://docs.rs#1811)#[derive(Default)]
[1812](https://docs.rs#1812)struct SeqInner {
[1813](https://docs.rs#1813)    /// Should match the `seq` field of the next [`SeqHandle`] that has not been
[1814](https://docs.rs#1814)    /// fully satisfied.
[1815](https://docs.rs#1815)    satisfaction_level: AtomicUsize,
[1816](https://docs.rs#1816)}
[1817](https://docs.rs#1817)
[1818](https://docs.rs#1818)impl SeqInner {
[1819](https://docs.rs#1819)    /// Record the call identified by `seq` as being called once.
[1820](https://docs.rs#1820)    fn called(&self, seq: usize, min_seq: usize, has_called_state: bool) {
[1821](https://docs.rs#1821)        let old_sl = self.satisfaction_level.fetch_max(
[1822](https://docs.rs#1822)            seq,
[1823](https://docs.rs#1823)            Ordering::Relaxed);
[1824](https://docs.rs#1824)        assert!(old_sl >= min_seq,
[1825](https://docs.rs#1825)            "Method sequence violation.  Method was called without preceding methods having been satisfied.");
[1826](https://docs.rs#1826)        assert!(old_sl <= seq + if has_called_state { 1 } else { 0 } ,
[1827](https://docs.rs#1827)            "Method sequence violation.  Method was called while succeeding methods have been called.");
[1828](https://docs.rs#1828)    }
[1829](https://docs.rs#1829)
[1830](https://docs.rs#1830)    /// Record the call identified by `seq` as fully satisfied.
[1831](https://docs.rs#1831)    fn satisfy(&self, seq: usize, min_seq: usize, has_called_state: bool) {
[1832](https://docs.rs#1832)        // Record that the SeqHandle identified by `seq` has been fully
[1833](https://docs.rs#1833)        // satisfied.  It is an error if some previous `SeqHandle` wasn't
[1834](https://docs.rs#1834)        // already satisfied.
[1835](https://docs.rs#1835)        let old_sl = self.satisfaction_level.fetch_max(
[1836](https://docs.rs#1836)            seq + if has_called_state { 1 } else { 0 },
[1837](https://docs.rs#1837)            Ordering::Relaxed);
[1838](https://docs.rs#1838)        assert!(old_sl >= min_seq,
[1839](https://docs.rs#1839)            "Method sequence violation.  Method was called without preceding methods having been satisfied.");
[1840](https://docs.rs#1840)        assert!(old_sl <= seq + if has_called_state { 1 } else { 0 } ,
[1841](https://docs.rs#1841)            "Method sequence violation.  Method was called while succeeding methods have been called.");
[1842](https://docs.rs#1842)    }
[1843](https://docs.rs#1843)
[1844](https://docs.rs#1844)    /// Verify that the call identified by `seq` was called in the correct order
[1845](https://docs.rs#1845)    fn verify<F: Fn() -> String>(
[1846](https://docs.rs#1846)        &self,
[1847](https://docs.rs#1847)        seq: usize,
[1848](https://docs.rs#1848)        min_seq: usize,
[1849](https://docs.rs#1849)        has_called_state: bool,
[1850](https://docs.rs#1850)        desc: F)
[1851](https://docs.rs#1851)    {
[1852](https://docs.rs#1852)        let current_level = self.satisfaction_level.load(
[1853](https://docs.rs#1853)            Ordering::Relaxed);
[1854](https://docs.rs#1854)        let max_seq = seq + if has_called_state { 1 } else { 0 };
[1855](https://docs.rs#1855)
[1856](https://docs.rs#1856)        assert!(current_level >= min_seq,
[1857](https://docs.rs#1857)            "{}: Method sequence violation", desc());
[1858](https://docs.rs#1858)        assert!(current_level <= max_seq,
[1859](https://docs.rs#1859)            "{}: Method sequence violation", desc());
[1860](https://docs.rs#1860)    }
[1861](https://docs.rs#1861)
[1862](https://docs.rs#1862)    fn is_history(&self, seq: usize, has_called_state: bool) -> bool {
[1863](https://docs.rs#1863)        let current_level = self.satisfaction_level.load(
[1864](https://docs.rs#1864)            Ordering::Relaxed);
[1865](https://docs.rs#1865)        let max_seq = seq + if has_called_state { 1 } else { 0 };
[1866](https://docs.rs#1866)
[1867](https://docs.rs#1867)        current_level > max_seq
[1868](https://docs.rs#1868)    }
[1869](https://docs.rs#1869)}
[1870](https://docs.rs#1870)
[1871](https://docs.rs#1871)/// Used to enforce that mock calls must happen in the sequence specified.
[1872](https://docs.rs#1872)///
[1873](https://docs.rs#1873)/// Sequences are performed greedily, and will try to use the earliest possible
[1874](https://docs.rs#1874)/// match.
[1875](https://docs.rs#1875)///
[1876](https://docs.rs#1876)/// # Examples
[1877](https://docs.rs#1877)/// ```
[1878](https://docs.rs#1878)/// # use mockall::*;
[1879](https://docs.rs#1879)/// #[automock]
[1880](https://docs.rs#1880)/// trait Foo {
[1881](https://docs.rs#1881)///     fn foo(&self);
[1882](https://docs.rs#1882)///     fn bar(&self) -> u32;
[1883](https://docs.rs#1883)/// }
[1884](https://docs.rs#1884)/// let mut seq = Sequence::new();
[1885](https://docs.rs#1885)///
[1886](https://docs.rs#1886)/// let mut mock0 = MockFoo::new();
[1887](https://docs.rs#1887)/// let mut mock1 = MockFoo::new();
[1888](https://docs.rs#1888)///
[1889](https://docs.rs#1889)/// mock0.expect_foo()
[1890](https://docs.rs#1890)///     .times(1)
[1891](https://docs.rs#1891)///     .returning(|| ())
[1892](https://docs.rs#1892)///     .in_sequence(&mut seq);
[1893](https://docs.rs#1893)///
[1894](https://docs.rs#1894)/// mock1.expect_bar()
[1895](https://docs.rs#1895)///     .times(1)
[1896](https://docs.rs#1896)///     .returning(|| 42)
[1897](https://docs.rs#1897)///     .in_sequence(&mut seq);
[1898](https://docs.rs#1898)///
[1899](https://docs.rs#1899)/// mock0.foo();
[1900](https://docs.rs#1900)/// mock1.bar();
[1901](https://docs.rs#1901)/// ```
[1902](https://docs.rs#1902)///
[1903](https://docs.rs#1903)/// The count is allowed to vary.
[1904](https://docs.rs#1904)/// ```
[1905](https://docs.rs#1905)/// # use mockall::*;
[1906](https://docs.rs#1906)/// #[automock]
[1907](https://docs.rs#1907)/// trait Foo {
[1908](https://docs.rs#1908)///     fn foo(&self);
[1909](https://docs.rs#1909)///     fn bar(&self) -> u32;
[1910](https://docs.rs#1910)/// }
[1911](https://docs.rs#1911)/// let mut seq = Sequence::new();
[1912](https://docs.rs#1912)///
[1913](https://docs.rs#1913)/// let mut mock0 = MockFoo::new();
[1914](https://docs.rs#1914)/// let mut mock1 = MockFoo::new();
[1915](https://docs.rs#1915)///
[1916](https://docs.rs#1916)/// mock0.expect_foo()
[1917](https://docs.rs#1917)///     .times(1..4)
[1918](https://docs.rs#1918)///     .returning(|| ())
[1919](https://docs.rs#1919)///     .in_sequence(&mut seq);
[1920](https://docs.rs#1920)///
[1921](https://docs.rs#1921)/// mock1.expect_bar()
[1922](https://docs.rs#1922)///     .times(1)
[1923](https://docs.rs#1923)///     .returning(|| 42)
[1924](https://docs.rs#1924)///     .in_sequence(&mut seq);
[1925](https://docs.rs#1925)///
[1926](https://docs.rs#1926)/// mock0.foo();
[1927](https://docs.rs#1927)/// mock0.foo();
[1928](https://docs.rs#1928)/// mock1.bar();
[1929](https://docs.rs#1929)/// ```
[1930](https://docs.rs#1930)///
[1931](https://docs.rs#1931)/// But, the previous count must be satisfied before a sequence may make
[1932](https://docs.rs#1932)/// progress.
[1933](https://docs.rs#1933)/// ```should_panic
[1934](https://docs.rs#1934)/// # use mockall::*;
[1935](https://docs.rs#1935)/// #[automock]
[1936](https://docs.rs#1936)/// trait Foo {
[1937](https://docs.rs#1937)///     fn foo(&self);
[1938](https://docs.rs#1938)///     fn bar(&self) -> u32;
[1939](https://docs.rs#1939)/// }
[1940](https://docs.rs#1940)/// let mut seq = Sequence::new();
[1941](https://docs.rs#1941)///
[1942](https://docs.rs#1942)/// let mut mock0 = MockFoo::new();
[1943](https://docs.rs#1943)/// let mut mock1 = MockFoo::new();
[1944](https://docs.rs#1944)///
[1945](https://docs.rs#1945)/// mock0.expect_foo()
[1946](https://docs.rs#1946)///     .times(3..5)
[1947](https://docs.rs#1947)///     .returning(|| ())
[1948](https://docs.rs#1948)///     .in_sequence(&mut seq);
[1949](https://docs.rs#1949)///
[1950](https://docs.rs#1950)/// mock1.expect_bar()
[1951](https://docs.rs#1951)///     .times(1)
[1952](https://docs.rs#1952)///     .returning(|| 42)
[1953](https://docs.rs#1953)///     .in_sequence(&mut seq);
[1954](https://docs.rs#1954)///
[1955](https://docs.rs#1955)/// mock0.foo();
[1956](https://docs.rs#1956)/// mock0.foo();
[1957](https://docs.rs#1957)/// mock1.bar();
[1958](https://docs.rs#1958)/// ```
[1959](https://docs.rs#1959)///
[1960](https://docs.rs#1960)/// Furthermore, sequences are greedy, and will only perform the earliest
[1961](https://docs.rs#1961)/// element in sequence that is allowed. This results in the following example
[1962](https://docs.rs#1962)/// failing the second expectation, as the first expectation is used for both
[1963](https://docs.rs#1963)/// calls to `foo`.
[1964](https://docs.rs#1964)///
[1965](https://docs.rs#1965)/// The following example fails as the first expection handles all calls,
[1966](https://docs.rs#1966)/// leaving none for the second expectation. As the second expectation goes
[1967](https://docs.rs#1967)/// unused, while it is expected to be called at least once, the test panics
[1968](https://docs.rs#1968)/// with
[1969](https://docs.rs#1969)/// `MockFoo::foo: Expectation(<anything>) called 0 time(s) which is fewer than
[1970](https://docs.rs#1970)/// expected 1`.
[1971](https://docs.rs#1971)///
[1972](https://docs.rs#1972)/// ```should_panic
[1973](https://docs.rs#1973)/// # use mockall::*;
[1974](https://docs.rs#1974)/// #[automock]
[1975](https://docs.rs#1975)/// trait Foo {
[1976](https://docs.rs#1976)///     fn foo(&self);
[1977](https://docs.rs#1977)///     fn bar(&self) -> u32;
[1978](https://docs.rs#1978)/// }
[1979](https://docs.rs#1979)/// let mut seq = Sequence::new();
[1980](https://docs.rs#1980)///
[1981](https://docs.rs#1981)/// let mut mock0 = MockFoo::new();
[1982](https://docs.rs#1982)///
[1983](https://docs.rs#1983)/// mock0.expect_foo()
[1984](https://docs.rs#1984)///     .returning(|| ())
[1985](https://docs.rs#1985)///     .in_sequence(&mut seq);
[1986](https://docs.rs#1986)///
[1987](https://docs.rs#1987)/// mock0.expect_foo()
[1988](https://docs.rs#1988)///     .times(1..)
[1989](https://docs.rs#1989)///     .returning(|| ())
[1990](https://docs.rs#1990)///     .in_sequence(&mut seq);
[1991](https://docs.rs#1991)///
[1992](https://docs.rs#1992)/// mock0.foo();
[1993](https://docs.rs#1993)/// mock0.foo();
[1994](https://docs.rs#1994)/// ```
[1995](https://docs.rs#1995)///
[1996](https://docs.rs#1996)#[derive(Default)]
[1997](https://docs.rs#1997)pub struct Sequence {
[1998](https://docs.rs#1998)    inner: Arc<SeqInner>,
[1999](https://docs.rs#1999)    /// Counter to use for the next SeqHandle associated with this Sequence
[2000](https://docs.rs#2000)    next_seq: usize,
[2001](https://docs.rs#2001)    next_min_seq: usize,
[2002](https://docs.rs#2002)}
[2003](https://docs.rs#2003)
[2004](https://docs.rs#2004)/// Indicates whether the minimum call count is zero, one or more.
[2005](https://docs.rs#2005)///
[2006](https://docs.rs#2006)/// Used to ensure the handle count is incremented accordingly.
[2007](https://docs.rs#2007)#[doc(hidden)]
[2008](https://docs.rs#2008)pub enum MinimumCallCount {
[2009](https://docs.rs#2009)    /// Method may never be called
[2010](https://docs.rs#2010)    Zero,
[2011](https://docs.rs#2011)    /// Method has to be called at least once
[2012](https://docs.rs#2012)    One,
[2013](https://docs.rs#2013)    /// Method has to be called more than once
[2014](https://docs.rs#2014)    More
[2015](https://docs.rs#2015)}
[2016](https://docs.rs#2016)
[2017](https://docs.rs#2017)/// Infer what the minimum call count is
[2018](https://docs.rs#2018)#[doc(hidden)]
[2019](https://docs.rs#2019)pub fn times_to_minimum_call_count(times: &Times) -> MinimumCallCount {
[2020](https://docs.rs#2020)    match times.minimum() {
[2021](https://docs.rs#2021)        0 => MinimumCallCount::Zero,
[2022](https://docs.rs#2022)        1 => MinimumCallCount::One,
[2023](https://docs.rs#2023)        _ => MinimumCallCount::More,
[2024](https://docs.rs#2024)    }
[2025](https://docs.rs#2025)}
[2026](https://docs.rs#2026)
[2027](https://docs.rs#2027)impl Sequence {
[2028](https://docs.rs#2028)    /// Create a new empty [`Sequence`]
[2029](https://docs.rs#2029)    pub fn new() -> Self {
[2030](https://docs.rs#2030)        Self::default()
[2031](https://docs.rs#2031)    }
[2032](https://docs.rs#2032)
[2033](https://docs.rs#2033)    /// Not for public consumption, but it must be public so the generated code
[2034](https://docs.rs#2034)    /// can call it.
[2035](https://docs.rs#2035)    #[doc(hidden)]
[2036](https://docs.rs#2036)    pub fn next_handle(
[2037](https://docs.rs#2037)        &mut self,
[2038](https://docs.rs#2038)        minimum_call_count: MinimumCallCount
[2039](https://docs.rs#2039)    ) -> SeqHandle
[2040](https://docs.rs#2040)    {
[2041](https://docs.rs#2041)        let has_called_state = match minimum_call_count {
[2042](https://docs.rs#2042)            // Is satisfied from the get-go, and does not need to differentiate
[2043](https://docs.rs#2043)            // between being called and satisfied.
[2044](https://docs.rs#2044)            MinimumCallCount::Zero => false,
[2045](https://docs.rs#2045)            // Need to differentiate between callable and satisfied if this
[2046](https://docs.rs#2046)            // is the first `[Expectation]` in a sequence. As it has to be
[2047](https://docs.rs#2047)            // called in order to be satisfied.
[2048](https://docs.rs#2048)            // For any later `[Expectation]`s the this initial callable state
[2049](https://docs.rs#2049)            // can be reused from the preceding  `[Expectation]`, because as
[2050](https://docs.rs#2050)            // soon as it is called, it is also satisfied.
[2051](https://docs.rs#2051)            MinimumCallCount::One if self.next_seq != 0 => false,
[2052](https://docs.rs#2052)            // If the count is two or more, after a single call the SeqHandle
[2053](https://docs.rs#2053)            // is in the called (but not satisfied) state.
[2054](https://docs.rs#2054)            _ => true,
[2055](https://docs.rs#2055)        };
[2056](https://docs.rs#2056)
[2057](https://docs.rs#2057)        let handle = SeqHandle {
[2058](https://docs.rs#2058)            inner: self.inner.clone(),
[2059](https://docs.rs#2059)            seq: self.next_seq,
[2060](https://docs.rs#2060)            min_seq: self.next_min_seq,
[2061](https://docs.rs#2061)            has_called_state
[2062](https://docs.rs#2062)        };
[2063](https://docs.rs#2063)
[2064](https://docs.rs#2064)        match minimum_call_count {
[2065](https://docs.rs#2065)            MinimumCallCount::Zero => {
[2066](https://docs.rs#2066)                // We don't update min_seq, as this `[Expectation]` can be
[2067](https://docs.rs#2067)                // skipped.
[2068](https://docs.rs#2068)                // Furthermore, as the call count can never be too low, only
[2069](https://docs.rs#2069)                // a Satisfied state is necessary for this handle.
[2070](https://docs.rs#2070)                self.next_seq += 1;
[2071](https://docs.rs#2071)            },
[2072](https://docs.rs#2072)            MinimumCallCount::One if self.next_seq != 0 => {
[2073](https://docs.rs#2073)                // We need to be in at least state next_seq to ensure this
[2074](https://docs.rs#2074)                // handle has been performed at least once.
[2075](https://docs.rs#2075)                self.next_min_seq = self.next_seq;
[2076](https://docs.rs#2076)                // Only need to have a (4) Satisfied state for this handle,
[2077](https://docs.rs#2077)                // as (3) Called does not occur.
[2078](https://docs.rs#2078)                self.next_seq += 1;
[2079](https://docs.rs#2079)            },
[2080](https://docs.rs#2080)            // MinimumCallCount::More, or MinimumCallCount::One for the very
[2081](https://docs.rs#2081)            // first element in sequence.
[2082](https://docs.rs#2082)            _ => {
[2083](https://docs.rs#2083)                // We need to be in at least state next_seq to ensure this
[2084](https://docs.rs#2084)                // handle has been performed at least once.
[2085](https://docs.rs#2085)                self.next_min_seq = self.next_seq + 1;
[2086](https://docs.rs#2086)                // next_seq is (3) Called for the current handle, next_seq + 1
[2087](https://docs.rs#2087)                // represents (4) Satisified.
[2088](https://docs.rs#2088)                self.next_seq += 2;
[2089](https://docs.rs#2089)            },
[2090](https://docs.rs#2090)        }
[2091](https://docs.rs#2091)        handle
[2092](https://docs.rs#2092)    }
[2093](https://docs.rs#2093)}

# automock in mockall - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/mockall/0.15.0/mockall/attr.automock.html

`#[automock]`## Expand description

Automatically generate mock types for structs and traits.

This is by far the easiest way to use Mockall.  It works on almost all
traits, and almost all structs that have a single `impl` block.  In either
case, it will generate a mock struct whose name is the name of the mocked
struct/trait prepended with “Mock”.  For each method of the original, the
mock struct will have a method named `expect_whatever` that allows you to
set expectations.  There will also be one `checkpoint` method that calls
[ checkpoint](https://docs.rs/mockall/index.html#checkpoints) for every single mocked method.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples)Examples

The simplest use case is mocking a no-frills trait

```
#[automock]
pub trait Foo {
    fn foo(&self, key: i16);
}
let mock = MockFoo::new();
```
Mocking a structure:

```
struct Foo {}
#[automock]
impl Foo {
    fn foo(&self) -> u32 {
        // ...
    }
}
```
You can also mock a trait impl on a struct:

```
pub trait Foo {
    fn foo(&self, key: i16);
}
struct Bar{}
#[automock]
impl Foo for Bar {
    fn foo(&self, key: i16){
        // ...
    }
}
let mock = MockBar::new();
```
Mocking a trait variant with a different name requires adding a metaitem to the attribute in order to mock the variant instead of the original:

```
#[automock(target = Foo)]
#[trait_variant::make(Foo: Send)]
trait LocalFoo {
    fn foo(&self) -> u32;
}
```
The example above demonstrates using `target = Foo`, which will generate
a `MockFoo` struct suitable for mocking the `Foo` variant.
Without `target = Foo`, `#[automock]` would have generated `MockLocalFoo`.

Mocking a trait with associated types requires adding a metaitem to the attribute:

```
#[automock(type Item=u32;)]
trait Foo {
    type Item;
    fn foo(&self) -> Self::Item;
}
```
It can mock a module full of functions.  In this case, the mock functions
will be found in a module whose name is prepended with `mock_`.

```
#[automock]
mod mymod {
    pub fn foo() -> u32 {
       // ...
    }
}
```
Finally, `#[automock]` can also mock foreign functions.  This works just
like mocking a module.

```
#[automock]
mod ffi {
    extern "C" {
        pub fn foo() -> u32;
    }
}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#limitations)Limitations

`#[automock]` can’t handle everything.  There are some cases where
you will need to use [ mock!](https://docs.rs/macro.mock.html) instead:

- Mocking a struct that has multiple `impl`blocks, including structs that implement traits.
- Mocking a struct or trait defined in another crate.
- Mocking a trait with trait bounds.
- If the autogenerated “MockFoo” name isn’t acceptable, and you want to choose your own name for the mock structure.

---

# mock in mockall - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/mockall/0.15.0/mockall/macro.mock.html

`mock!() { /* proc-macro */ }`## Expand description

Manually mock a structure.

Sometimes [ automock](https://docs.rs/attr.automock.html) can’t be used.  In those cases you can use

`mock!`,
which basically involves repeating the struct’s or trait’s definitions.The format is:

- Optional visibility specifier
- Real structure name and generics fields
- 0 or more methods of the structure, written without bodies, enclosed in a {} block
- 0 or more impl blocks implementing traits on the structure, also without bodies.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples)Examples

Mock a trait. This is the simplest use case.

```
trait Foo {
    fn foo(&self, x: u32);
}
mock!{
    pub MyStruct<T: Clone + 'static> {
        fn bar(&self) -> u8;
    }
    impl<T: Clone + 'static> Foo for MyStruct<T> {
        fn foo(&self, x: u32);
    }
}
```
Mocking an unsupported `#[derive(X)]` attribute, e.g. [ Clone](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/clone/trait.Clone.html), is
similar.

```
#[derive(Clone)]
struct MyStruct;
mock!{
    pub MyStruct {
        fn bar(&self);
    }
    impl Clone for MyStruct {
        fn clone(&self) -> Self;
    }
}
```
When mocking a generic struct’s implementation of a generic trait, use the
same name for their generic parameters.  For example, if you wanted to mock
`Rc`, do

```
mock!{
    pub Rc<T> {}
    impl<T> AsRef<T> for Rc<T> {
        fn as_ref(&self) -> &T;
    }
}
```
*not*

Associated types can easily be mocked by specifying a concrete type in the
`mock!{}` invocation.

```
mock!{
    MyIter {}
    impl Iterator for MyIter {
        type Item=u32;
        fn next(&mut self) -> Option<<Self as Iterator>::Item>;
    }
}
```

# Sequence in mockall - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/mockall/0.15.0/mockall/struct.Sequence.html

`pub struct Sequence { /* private fields */ }`## Expand description

Used to enforce that mock calls must happen in the sequence specified.

Sequences are performed greedily, and will try to use the earliest possible match.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples)Examples

```
#[automock]
trait Foo {
    fn foo(&self);
    fn bar(&self) -> u32;
}
let mut seq = Sequence::new();
let mut mock0 = MockFoo::new();
let mut mock1 = MockFoo::new();
mock0.expect_foo()
    .times(1)
    .returning(|| ())
    .in_sequence(&mut seq);
mock1.expect_bar()
    .times(1)
    .returning(|| 42)
    .in_sequence(&mut seq);
mock0.foo();
mock1.bar();
```
The count is allowed to vary.

```
#[automock]
trait Foo {
    fn foo(&self);
    fn bar(&self) -> u32;
}
let mut seq = Sequence::new();
let mut mock0 = MockFoo::new();
let mut mock1 = MockFoo::new();
mock0.expect_foo()
    .times(1..4)
    .returning(|| ())
    .in_sequence(&mut seq);
mock1.expect_bar()
    .times(1)
    .returning(|| 42)
    .in_sequence(&mut seq);
mock0.foo();
mock0.foo();
mock1.bar();
```
But, the previous count must be satisfied before a sequence may make progress.

[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
#[automock]
trait Foo {
    fn foo(&self);
    fn bar(&self) -> u32;
}
let mut seq = Sequence::new();
let mut mock0 = MockFoo::new();
let mut mock1 = MockFoo::new();
mock0.expect_foo()
    .times(3..5)
    .returning(|| ())
    .in_sequence(&mut seq);
mock1.expect_bar()
    .times(1)
    .returning(|| 42)
    .in_sequence(&mut seq);
mock0.foo();
mock0.foo();
mock1.bar();
```
Furthermore, sequences are greedy, and will only perform the earliest
element in sequence that is allowed. This results in the following example
failing the second expectation, as the first expectation is used for both
calls to `foo`.

The following example fails as the first expection handles all calls,
leaving none for the second expectation. As the second expectation goes
unused, while it is expected to be called at least once, the test panics
with
`MockFoo::foo: Expectation(<anything>) called 0 time(s) which is fewer than expected 1`.

[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
#[automock]
trait Foo {
    fn foo(&self);
    fn bar(&self) -> u32;
}
let mut seq = Sequence::new();
let mut mock0 = MockFoo::new();
mock0.expect_foo()
    .returning(|| ())
    .in_sequence(&mut seq);
mock0.expect_foo()
    .times(1..)
    .returning(|| ())
    .in_sequence(&mut seq);
mock0.foo();
mock0.foo();
```

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/mockall/examples.rs.html#8)#### pub fn [returning_st](https://docs.rs#method.returning_st)<MockallF>(&mut self, __mockall_f: MockallF) -> &mut Self

Single-threaded version of [ returning](https://docs.rs#method.returning).
Can be used when the argument or return type isn’t

`Send`.It is a runtime error to call the mock method from a different thread than the one that originally called this method.

Restrict the number of times that that this method may be called.

The argument may be:

- A fixed number: `.times(4)`
- Various types of range:
- `.times(5..10)`
- `.times(..10)`
- `.times(5..)`
- `.times(5..=10)`
- `.times(..=10)`

- The wildcard: `.times(..)`

    // Required method
    fn [eval](https://docs.rs#tymethod.eval)(&self, variable: [&Item](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.reference.html)) -> [bool](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.bool.html);
    // Provided method
    fn [find_case](https://docs.rs#method.find_case)<'a>(
        &'a self,
        expected: [bool](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.bool.html),
        variable: [&Item](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.reference.html),
    ) -> [Option](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/option/enum.Option.html)<[Case](https://docs.rs/predicates-core/1.0.10/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/predicates_core/reflection/struct.Case.html)<'a>> { ... }
}## Expand description

Trait for generically evaluating a type against a dynamically created predicate function.

The exact meaning of `eval` depends on the situation, but will usually
mean that the evaluated item is in some sort of pre-defined set.  This is
different from `Ord` and `Eq` in that an `item` will almost never be the
same type as the implementing `Predicate` type.

## Required Methods[§](https://docs.rs#required-methods)

## Provided Methods[§](https://docs.rs#provided-methods)

## Dyn Compatibility[§](https://docs.rs#dyn-compatibility)

*In older versions of Rust, dyn compatibility was called "object safety".*

# function in mockall::predicate - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/mockall/0.15.0/mockall/predicate/fn.function.html

`pub fn function<F, T>(function: F) -> `[FnPredicate](https://docs.rs/predicates/3.1.4/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/predicates/function/struct.FnPredicate.html)<F, T>## Expand description

Creates a new predicate that wraps over the given function. The returned
type implements `Predicate` and therefore has all combinators available to
it.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples)Examples

```
use predicates::prelude::*;
struct Example {
    string: String,
    number: i32,
}
let string_check = predicate::function(|x: &Example| x.string == "hello");
let number_check = predicate::function(|x: &Example| x.number == 42);
let predicate_fn = string_check.and(number_check);
let good_example = Example { string: "hello".into(), number: 42 };
assert_eq!(true, predicate_fn.eval(&good_example));
let bad_example = Example { string: "goodbye".into(), number: 0 };
assert_eq!(false, predicate_fn.eval(&bad_example));
```

# mockall - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/mockall/latest/mockall/

## Expand description

A powerful mock object library for Rust.

Mockall provides tools to create mock versions of almost any trait or struct. They can be used in unit tests as a stand-in for the real object.

[§](https://docs.rs#usage)Usage

There are two ways to use Mockall.  The easiest is to use
[ #[automock]](https://docs.rs/attr.automock.html).  It can mock most traits, or structs
that only have a single

`impl` block.  For things it can’t handle, there is
[.](https://docs.rs/macro.mock.html)

`mock!`Whichever method is used, the basic idea is the same.

- Create a mock struct. It’s name will be the same as the original, with “Mock” prepended.
- In your test, instantiate the mock struct with its `new`or`default`method.
- Set expectations on the mock struct.  Each expectation can have required
argument matchers, a required call count, and a required position in a
`Sequence`
- Supply the mock object to the code that you’re testing. It will return the preprogrammed return values supplied in the previous step. Any accesses contrary to your expectations will cause a panic.

[§](https://docs.rs#user-guide)User Guide

- `Getting started`
- `Static Return values`
- `Matching arguments`
- `Call counts`
- `Sequences`
- `Checkpoints`
- `Reference arguments`
- `Reference return values`
- `impl Trait`
- `Mocking structs`
- `Generic methods`
- `Generic traits and structs`
- `Associated types`
- `Multiple and inherited traits`
- `External traits`
- `Static methods`
- `Modules`
- `Foreign functions`
- `Debug`
- `Async Traits`
- `Crate features`
- `Examples`

[§](https://docs.rs#getting-started)Getting Started

```
use mockall::*;
use mockall::predicate::*;
#[automock]
trait MyTrait {
    fn foo(&self, x: u32) -> u32;
}
fn call_with_four(x: &dyn MyTrait) -> u32 {
    x.foo(4)
}
let mut mock = MockMyTrait::new();
mock.expect_foo()
    .with(predicate::eq(4))
    .times(1)
    .returning(|x| x + 1);
assert_eq!(5, call_with_four(&mock));
```
[§](https://docs.rs#static-return-values)Static Return values

Every expectation must have an associated return value (though when the
**nightly** feature is enabled expectations will automatically return the
default values of their return types, if their return types implement
`Default`.).  For methods that return a `static` value, the macros will
generate an `Expectation` struct like
[ this](https://docs.rs/examples/__mock_MockFoo_Foo/__foo/struct.Expectation.html).
There are two ways to set such an expectation’s return value: with a
constant
(

[) or a closure (](https://docs.rs/examples/__mock_MockFoo_Foo/__foo/struct.Expectation.html#method.return_const)

`return_const`[). A closure will take the method’s arguments by value.](https://docs.rs/examples/__mock_MockFoo_Foo/__foo/struct.Expectation.html#method.returning)

`returning````
#[automock]
trait MyTrait {
    fn foo(&self) -> u32;
    fn bar(&self, x: u32, y: u32) -> u32;
}
let mut mock = MockMyTrait::new();
mock.expect_foo()
    .return_const(42u32);
mock.expect_bar()
    .returning(|x, y| x + y);
```
Additionally, constants that aren’t `Clone` can be returned with the
[ return_once](https://docs.rs/examples/__mock_MockFoo_Foo/__foo/struct.Expectation.html#method.return_once)
method.

```
struct NonClone();
#[automock]
trait Foo {
    fn foo(&self) -> NonClone;
}
let mut mock = MockFoo::new();
let r = NonClone{};
mock.expect_foo()
    .return_once(move || r);
```
`return_once` can also be used for computing the return value with an
`FnOnce` closure.  This is useful for returning a non-`Clone` value and also
triggering side effects at the same time.

```
fn do_something() {}
struct NonClone();
#[automock]
trait Foo {
    fn foo(&self) -> NonClone;
}
let mut mock = MockFoo::new();
let r = NonClone{};
mock.expect_foo()
    .return_once(move || {
        do_something();
        r
    });
```
Mock objects are always `Send`.  If you need to use a return type that
isn’t, you can use the
[ return_const_st](https://docs.rs/examples/__mock_MockFoo_Foo/__foo/struct.Expectation.html#method.return_const_st),

[, or](https://docs.rs/examples/__mock_MockFoo_Foo/__foo/struct.Expectation.html#method.returning_st)

`returning_st`[, methods. If you need to match arguments that are not](https://docs.rs/examples/__mock_MockFoo_Foo/__foo/struct.Expectation.html#method.return_once_st)

`return_once_st``Send`, you can use the
[These take a non-](https://docs.rs/examples/__mock_MockFoo_Foo/__foo/struct.Expectation.html#method.withf_st)

`withf_st``Send` object and add runtime access checks.  The wrapped
object will be `Send`, but accessing it from multiple threads will cause a
runtime panic.```
#[automock]
trait Foo {
    fn foo(&self, x: Rc<u32>) -> Rc<u32>;   // Rc<u32> isn't Send
}
let mut mock = MockFoo::new();
let x = Rc::new(5);
let argument = x.clone();
mock.expect_foo()
    .withf_st(move |x| *x == argument)
    .returning_st(move |_| Rc::new(42u32));
assert_eq!(42, *mock.foo(x));
```
[§](https://docs.rs#matching-arguments)Matching arguments

Optionally, expectations may have argument matchers set.  A matcher will
verify that the expectation was called with the expected arguments, or panic
otherwise.  A matcher is anything that implements the [ Predicate](https://docs.rs/trait.Predicate.html) trait.
For example:

[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
#[automock]
trait Foo {
    fn foo(&self, x: u32);
}
let mut mock = MockFoo::new();
mock.expect_foo()
    .with(eq(42))
    .return_const(());
mock.foo(0);    // Panics!
```
See [ predicate](https://docs.rs/trait.Predicate.html) for a list of Mockall’s builtin predicate functions.
For convenience,

[is a shorthand for setting the commonly used](https://docs.rs/examples/__mock_MockFoo_Foo/__foo/struct.Expectation.html#method.withf)

`withf`[predicate. The arguments to the predicate function are the method’s arguments,](https://docs.rs/predicate/fn.function.html)

`function`*by reference*. For example:

[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
#[automock]
trait Foo {
    fn foo(&self, x: u32, y: u32);
}
let mut mock = MockFoo::new();
mock.expect_foo()
    .withf(|x: &u32, y: &u32| x == y)
    .return_const(());
mock.foo(2 + 2, 5);    // Panics!
```
[§](https://docs.rs#matching-multiple-calls)Matching multiple calls

Matchers can also be used to discriminate between different invocations of the same function. Used that way, they can provide different return values for different arguments. The way this works is that on a method call, all expectations set on a given method are evaluated in FIFO order. The first matching expectation is used. Only if none of the expectations match does Mockall panic. For example:

```
#[automock]
trait Foo {
    fn foo(&self, x: u32) -> u32;
}
let mut mock = MockFoo::new();
mock.expect_foo()
    .with(eq(5))
    .return_const(50u32);
mock.expect_foo()
    .with(eq(6))
    .return_const(60u32);
```
One common pattern is to use multiple expectations in order of decreasing specificity. The last expectation can provide a default or fallback value, and earlier ones can be more specific. For example:

```
#[automock]
trait Foo {
    fn open(&self, path: String) -> Option<u32>;
}
let mut mock = MockFoo::new();
mock.expect_open()
    .with(eq(String::from("something.txt")))
    .returning(|_| Some(5));
mock.expect_open()
    .return_const(None);
```
[§](https://docs.rs#call-counts)Call counts

By default, every expectation is allowed to be called an unlimited number of times. But Mockall can optionally verify that an expectation was called a fixed number of times, or any number of times within a given range.

[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
#[automock]
trait Foo {
    fn foo(&self, x: u32);
}
let mut mock = MockFoo::new();
mock.expect_foo()
    .times(1)
    .return_const(());
mock.foo(0);    // Ok
mock.foo(1);    // Panics!
```
[§](https://docs.rs#sequences)Sequences

By default expectations may be matched in any order.  But it’s possible to
specify the order by using a [ Sequence](https://docs.rs/struct.Sequence.html).  Any expectations may be added to
the same sequence.  They don’t even need to come from the same object.

[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
#[automock]
trait Foo {
    fn foo(&self);
}
let mut seq = Sequence::new();
let mut mock1 = MockFoo::new();
mock1.expect_foo()
    .times(1)
    .in_sequence(&mut seq)
    .returning(|| ());
let mut mock2 = MockFoo::new();
mock2.expect_foo()
    .times(1)
    .in_sequence(&mut seq)
    .returning(|| ());
mock2.foo();    // Panics!  mock1.foo should've been called first.
```
[§](https://docs.rs#checkpoints)Checkpoints

Sometimes its useful to validate all expectations mid-test, throw them away,
and add new ones.  That’s what checkpoints do.  Every mock object has a
`checkpoint` method.  When called, it will immediately validate all methods’
expectations.  So any expectations that haven’t satisfied their call count
will panic.  Afterwards, those expectations will be cleared so you can add
new expectations and keep testing.

[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
#[automock]
trait Foo {
    fn foo(&self);
}
let mut mock = MockFoo::new();
mock.expect_foo()
    .times(2)
    .returning(|| ());
mock.foo();
mock.checkpoint();  // Panics!  foo hasn't yet been called twice.
```
[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
#[automock]
trait Foo {
    fn foo(&self);
}
let mut mock = MockFoo::new();
mock.expect_foo()
    .times(1)
    .returning(|| ());
mock.foo();
mock.checkpoint();
mock.foo();         // Panics!  The expectation has been cleared.
```
[§](https://docs.rs#reference-arguments)Reference arguments

Mockall can mock methods with reference arguments, too.  There’s one catch:
the matcher [ Predicate](https://docs.rs/trait.Predicate.html) will take reference arguments by value, not by
reference.

```
#[automock]
trait Foo {
    fn foo(&self, x: &u32) -> u32;
}
let mut mock = MockFoo::new();
let e = mock.expect_foo()
    // Note that x is a &u32, not a &&u32
    .withf(|x: &u32| *x == 5)
    .returning(|x: &u32| *x + 1);
assert_eq!(6, mock.foo(&5));
```
[§](https://docs.rs#reference-return-values)Reference return values

Mockall can also use reference return values.  There is one restriction: the
lifetime of the returned reference must be either the same as the lifetime
of the mock object, or `'static`.

Mockall creates different expectation types for methods that return
references.  Their API is the same as the basic `Expectation`, except for
setting return values.

Methods that return `'static` references work just like methods that return
any other `'static` value.

```
struct Thing(u32);
#[automock]
trait Container {
    fn get(&self, i: u32) -> &'static Thing;
}
const THING: Thing = Thing(42);
let mut mock = MockContainer::new();
mock.expect_get()
    .return_const(&THING);
assert_eq!(42, mock.get(0).0);
```
Methods that take a `&self` argument use an `Expectation` class like
[this](https://docs.rs/examples/__mock_MockFoo_Foo/__bar/struct.Expectation.html),
which
gets its return value from the
[ return_const](https://docs.rs/examples/__mock_MockFoo_Foo/__bar/struct.Expectation.html#method.return_const) method.

```
struct Thing(u32);
#[automock]
trait Container {
    fn get(&self, i: u32) -> &Thing;
}
let thing = Thing(42);
let mut mock = MockContainer::new();
mock.expect_get()
    .return_const(thing);
assert_eq!(42, mock.get(0).0);
```
Methods that take a `&mut self` argument use an `Expectation` class like
[this](https://docs.rs/examples/__mock_MockFoo_Foo/__baz/struct.Expectation.html),
class, regardless of whether the return value is actually mutable.  They can
take their return value either from the
[ return_var](https://docs.rs/examples/__mock_MockFoo_Foo/__baz/struct.Expectation.html#method.return_var)
or

[methods.](https://docs.rs/examples/__mock_MockFoo_Foo/__baz/struct.Expectation.html#method.returning)

`returning````
struct Thing(u32);
#[automock]
trait Container {
    fn get_mut(&mut self, i: u32) -> &mut Thing;
}
let thing = Thing(42);
let mut mock = MockContainer::new();
mock.expect_get_mut()
    .return_var(thing);
mock.get_mut(0).0 = 43;
assert_eq!(43, mock.get_mut(0).0);
```
Unsized types that are common targets for
[ Deref](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/ops/deref/trait.Deref.html)
are special.  Mockall
will automatically use the type’s owned form for the Expectation.
Currently, the

[,](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/ffi/c_str/struct.CStr.html)

`CStr`[,](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/ffi/os_str/struct.OsStr.html)

`OsStr`[,](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/path/struct.Path.html)

`Path`[, and](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/alloc/slice/index.html)

`Slice`[types are supported. Using this feature is automatic:](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/alloc/str/index.html)

`str````
#[automock]
trait Foo {
    fn name(&self) -> &str;
}
let mut mock = MockFoo::new();
mock.expect_name().return_const("abcd".to_owned());
assert_eq!("abcd", mock.name());
```
Similarly, Mockall will use a Boxed trait object for the Expectation of methods that return references to trait objects.

```
#[automock]
trait Foo {
    fn name(&self) -> &dyn Display;
}
let mut mock = MockFoo::new();
mock.expect_name().return_const(Box::new("abcd"));
assert_eq!("abcd", format!("{}", mock.name()));
```
[§](https://docs.rs#impl-trait)Impl Trait

Rust 1.26.0 introduced the `impl Trait` feature.  It allows functions to
return concrete but unnamed types (and, less usefully, to take them as
arguments).  It’s *almost* the same as `Box<dyn Trait>` but without the
extra allocation.  Mockall supports deriving mocks for methods that return
`impl Trait`, with limitations.  When you derive the mock for such a method,
Mockall internally transforms the Expectation’s return type to `Box<dyn Trait>`, without changing the mock method’s signature.  So you can use it
like this:

```
struct Foo {}
#[automock]
impl Foo {
    fn foo(&self) -> impl Debug {
        // ...
    }
}
let mut mock = MockFoo::new();
mock.expect_foo()
    .returning(|| Box::new(String::from("Hello, World!")));
println!("{:?}", mock.foo());
```
However, `impl Trait` isn’t *exactly* equivalent to `Box<dyn Trait>` but
with fewer allocations.  There are some things the former can do but the
latter can’t.  For one thing, you can’t build a trait object out of a
`Sized` trait.  So this won’t work:

Nor can you create a trait object that implements two or more non-auto types. So this won’t work either:

For such cases, there is no magic bullet. The best way to mock methods like those would be to refactor them to return named (but possibly opaque) types instead.

See Also `impl-trait-for-returning-complex-types-with-ease.html`

[§](https://docs.rs#impl-future)impl Future

Rust 1.36.0 added the `Future` trait.  Unlike virtually every trait that
preceeded it, `Box<dyn Future>` is mostly useless.  Instead, you usually
need a `Pin<Box<dyn Future>>`.  So that’s what Mockall will do when you mock
a method returning `impl Future` or the related `impl Stream`.  Just
remember to use `pin` in your expectations, like this:

```
struct Foo {}
#[automock]
impl Foo {
    fn foo(&self) -> impl Future<Output=i32> {
        // ...
    }
}
let mut mock = MockFoo::new();
mock.expect_foo()
    .returning(|| Box::pin(future::ready(42)));
```
[§](https://docs.rs#mocking-structs)Mocking structs

Mockall mocks structs as well as traits.  The problem here is a namespace
problem: it’s hard to supply the mock object to your code under test,
because it has a different name.  The solution is to alter import paths
during test.  The easiest way to do that is with the
[ mockall_double](https://docs.rs/mockall_double/latest) crate.

[ #[automock]](https://docs.rs/attr.automock.html)
works for structs that have a single

`impl` block:```
use mockall_double::double;
mod thing {
    use mockall::automock;
    pub struct Thing{}
    #[automock]
    impl Thing {
        pub fn foo(&self) -> u32 {
            // ...
        }
    }
}
#[double]
use thing::Thing;
fn do_stuff(thing: &Thing) -> u32 {
    thing.foo()
}
#[cfg(test)]
mod t {
    use super::*;
    #[test]
    fn test_foo() {
        let mut mock = Thing::default();
        mock.expect_foo().returning(|| 42);
        do_stuff(&mock);
    }
}
```
For structs with more than one `impl` block or that have unsupported
`#[derive(X)]` attributes, e.g. `Clone`, see [ mock!](https://docs.rs/macro.mock.html) instead.

[§](https://docs.rs#generic-methods)Generic methods

Mocking generic methods is possible, but the exact process depends on
whether the parameters are `'static`, non-`'static`, or lifetimes.

[§](https://docs.rs#with-static-parameters)With static parameters

With fully `'static` parameters, the mock method is generic and so is its
expect_* method.  The expect_* method usually must be called with a
turbofish.  Expectations set with different generic parameters operate
completely independently of one another.

```
#[automock]
trait Foo {
    fn foo<T: 'static>(&self, t: T) -> i32;
}
let mut mock = MockFoo::new();
mock.expect_foo::<i16>()
    .returning(|t| i32::from(t));
mock.expect_foo::<i8>()
    .returning(|t| -i32::from(t));
assert_eq!(5, mock.foo(5i16));
assert_eq!(-5, mock.foo(5i8));
```
[§](https://docs.rs#with-non-static-type-parameters)With non-`static` type parameters

Mocking methods with non-`'static` type parameters is harder.  The way
Mockall does it is by turning the generic parameters into trait objects
before evaluating expectations.  This makes the expect_* method concrete,
rather than generic.  It also comes with many restrictions.  See
[ #[concretize]](https://docs.rs/attr.concretize.html) for more details.

[§](https://docs.rs#with-generic-lifetimes)With generic lifetimes

A method with a lifetime parameter is technically a generic method, but
Mockall treats it like a non-generic method that must work for all possible
lifetimes.  Mocking such a method is similar to mocking a non-generic
method, with a few additional restrictions.  One restriction is that you
can’t match calls with `with`, you must use `withf` instead.  Another is
that the generic lifetime may not appear as part of the return type.
Finally, no method may have both generic lifetime parameters *and* generic
type parameters.

```
struct X<'a>(&'a i32);
#[automock]
trait Foo {
    fn foo<'a>(&self, x: X<'a>) -> i32;
}
let mut mock = MockFoo::new();
mock.expect_foo()
    .withf(|f| *f.0 == 5)
    .return_const(42);
let x = X(&5);
assert_eq!(42, mock.foo(x));
```
[§](https://docs.rs#generic-traits-and-structs)Generic traits and structs

Mocking generic structs and generic traits is not a problem.  The mock
struct will be generic, too.  As with generic methods, lifetime parameters
are not allowed.  However, as long as the generic parameters are not used by
any static methods, then the parameters need not be `'static'`.

```
#[automock]
trait Foo<T> {
    fn foo(&self, t: T) -> i32;
}
let mut mock = MockFoo::<i16>::new();
mock.expect_foo()
    .returning(|t| i32::from(t));
assert_eq!(5, mock.foo(5i16));
```
[§](https://docs.rs#associated-types)Associated types

Traits with associated types can be mocked too.  Unlike generic traits, the
mock struct will not be generic.  Instead, you must specify the associated
types when defining the mock struct.  They’re specified as metaitems to the
[ #[automock]](https://docs.rs/attr.automock.html) attribute.

```
#[automock(type Key=u16; type Value=i32;)]
pub trait A {
    type Key;
    type Value;
    fn foo(&self, k: Self::Key) -> Self::Value;
}
let mut mock = MockA::new();
mock.expect_foo()
    .returning(|x: u16| i32::from(x));
assert_eq!(4, mock.foo(4));
```
[§](https://docs.rs#multiple-and-inherited-traits)Multiple and inherited traits

Creating a mock struct that implements multiple traits, whether inherited or
not, requires using the [ mock!](https://docs.rs/macro.mock.html) macro.  But once created,
using it is just the same as using any other mock object:

```
pub trait A {
    fn foo(&self);
}
pub trait B: A {
    fn bar(&self);
}
mock! {
    // Structure to mock
    C {}
    // First trait to implement on C
    impl A for C {
        fn foo(&self);
    }
    // Second trait to implement on C
    impl B for C {
        fn bar(&self);
    }
}
let mut mock = MockC::new();
mock.expect_foo().returning(|| ());
mock.expect_bar().returning(|| ());
mock.foo();
mock.bar();
```
[§](https://docs.rs#external-traits)External traits

Mockall can mock traits and structs defined in external crates that are
beyond your control, but you must use [ mock!](https://docs.rs/macro.mock.html) instead of

[. Mock an external trait like this:](https://docs.rs/attr.automock.html)

`#[automock]````
mock! {
    MyStruct {}     // Name of the mock struct, less the "Mock" prefix
    impl Clone for MyStruct {   // specification of the trait to mock
        fn clone(&self) -> Self;
    }
}
let mut mock1 = MockMyStruct::new();
let mock2 = MockMyStruct::new();
mock1.expect_clone()
    .return_once(move || mock2);
let cloned = mock1.clone();
```
[§](https://docs.rs#static-methods)Static methods

Mockall can also mock static methods.  But be careful!  The expectations are
global.  If you want to use a static method in multiple tests, you must
provide your own synchronization. See the [ synchronization example](https://github.com/asomers/mockall/blob/master/mockall/examples/synchronization.rs)
for a basic implementation. For ordinary methods, expectations are
set on the mock object.  But static methods don’t have any mock object.
Instead, you must create a

`Context` object just to set their expectations.```
#[automock]
pub trait A {
    fn foo() -> u32;
}
let ctx = MockA::foo_context();
ctx.expect().returning(|| 99);
assert_eq!(99, MockA::foo());
```
A common pattern is mocking a trait with a constructor method. In this case, you can easily set the mock constructor method to return a mock object.

```
struct Foo{}
#[automock]
impl Foo {
    fn from_i32(x: i32) -> Self {
        // ...
    }
    fn foo(&self) -> i32 {
        // ...
    }
}
let ctx = MockFoo::from_i32_context();
ctx.expect()
    .returning(|x| {
        let mut mock = MockFoo::default();
        mock.expect_foo()
            .return_const(x);
        mock
    });
let foo = MockFoo::from_i32(42);
assert_eq!(42, foo.foo());
```
[§](https://docs.rs#generic-static-methods)Generic static methods

Mocking static methods of generic structs or traits, whether or not the
methods themselves are generic, should work seamlessly as long as the
generic parameter is `'static`

```
#[automock]
trait Foo<T: 'static> {
    fn new(t: T) -> MockFoo<T>;
}
let ctx = MockFoo::<u32>::new_context();
ctx.expect()
    .returning(|_| MockFoo::default());
let mock = MockFoo::<u32>::new(42u32);
```
[§](https://docs.rs#context-checkpoints)Context checkpoints

The context object cleans up all expectations when it leaves scope.  It also
has a `checkpoint` method that functions just like a mock object’s
`checkpoint` method.

[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
#[automock]
pub trait A {
    fn foo() -> u32;
}
let ctx = MockA::foo_context();
ctx.expect()
    .times(1)
    .returning(|| 99);
ctx.checkpoint();   // Panics!
```
A mock object’s checkpoint method does *not* checkpoint static methods.
This behavior is useful when using multiple mock objects at once.  For
example:

```
#[automock]
pub trait A {
    fn build() -> Self;
    fn bar(&self) -> i32;
}
let ctx = MockA::build_context();
ctx.expect()
    .times(2)
    .returning(|| MockA::default());
let mut mock0 = MockA::build();
mock0.expect_bar().return_const(4);
mock0.bar();
mock0.checkpoint();     // Does not checkpoint the build method
let mock1 = MockA::build();
```
One more thing: Mockall normally creates a zero-argument `new` method for
every mock struct.  But it *won’t* do that when mocking a struct that
already has a method named `new`.  The `default` method will still be
present.

[§](https://docs.rs#modules)Modules

In addition to mocking types, Mockall can also derive mocks for
entire modules of Rust functions.  Mockall will generate a new module named
“mock_xxx”, if “xxx” is the original module’s name.  You can also use
`#[double]` to selectively import the mock module.

Be careful!  Module functions are static and so have the same caveats as
[static methods](https://docs.rs#static-methods) described above.

```
mod outer {
    use mockall::automock;
    #[automock()]
    pub(super) mod inner {
        pub fn bar(x: u32) -> i64 {
            // ...
        }
    }
}
#[double]
use outer::inner;
#[cfg(test)]
mod t {
    use super::*;
    #[test]
    fn test_foo_bar() {
        let ctx = inner::bar_context();
        ctx.expect()
            .returning(|x| i64::from(x + 1));
        assert_eq!(5, inner::bar(4));
    }
}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#foreign-functions)Foreign functions

One reason to mock modules is when working with foreign functions. Modules may contain foreign functions, even though structs and traits may not. Like static methods, the expectations are global.

```
mod outer {
    #[automock]
    pub mod ffi {
        extern "C" {
            pub fn foo(x: u32) -> i64;
        }
    }
}
#[double]
use outer::ffi;
fn do_stuff() -> i64 {
    unsafe{ ffi::foo(42) }
}
#[cfg(test)]
mod t {
    use super::*;
    #[test]
    fn test_foo() {
        let ctx = ffi::foo_context();
        ctx.expect()
            .returning(|x| i64::from(x + 1));
        assert_eq!(43, do_stuff());
    }
}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#debug)Debug

`#[automock]` will automatically generate `Debug` impls when mocking traits
and struct impls.  `mock!` will too, if you add a `#[derive(Debug)]`, like
this:

```
mock! {
    #[derive(Debug)]
    pub Foo {}
}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#async-traits)Async Traits

Partial support for async traits was introduced in the Rust language since
1.75.0.
Mockall is compatible with them, as well as both
[ async_trait](https://docs.rs/async-trait/latest/async_trait/) and

[crates, with two important limitations:](https://docs.rs/trait-variant/latest/trait_variant/)

`trait_variant`-
The `#[automock]`attribute must appear*before*the crate’s attribute.
-
The `#[async_trait]`and`#[trait_variant::make]`macros must be imported with their canonical names.

```
// async_trait works with both #[automock]
#[automock]
#[async_trait]
pub trait Foo {
   async fn foo(&self) -> u32;
}
// and mock!
mock! {
    pub Bar {}
    #[async_trait]
    impl Foo for Bar {
        async fn foo(&self) -> u32;
    }
}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#crate-features)Crate features

Mockall has a **nightly** feature.  Currently this feature has two
effects:

-
The compiler will produce better error messages.
-
Expectations for methods whose return type implements `Default`needn’t have their return values explicitly set. Instead, they will automatically return the default value.

With **nightly** enabled, you can omit the return value like this:

```
#[automock]
trait Foo {
    fn foo(&self) -> Vec<u32>;
}
let mut mock = MockFoo::new();
mock.expect_foo();
assert!(mock.foo().is_empty());
```

# fragile 2.1.0 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/fragile/^2.0

# Fragile

This library provides wrapper types that permit sending non Send types to other threads and use runtime checks to ensure safety.

It provides the `Fragile<T>`, `Sticky<T>` and `SemiSticky<T>` types which are
similar in nature but have different behaviors with regards to how destructors
are executed.  The `Fragile<T>` will panic if the destructor is called in another
thread, `Sticky<T>` will temporarily leak the object until the thread shuts down.
`SemiSticky<T>` is a compromise of the two.  It behaves like `Sticky<T>` but it
avoids the use of thread local storage if the type does not need `Drop`.

## Example

```
use thread;
// creating and using a fragile object in the same thread works
let val = new;
assert_eq!;
assert!;
// once send to another thread it stops working
spawn.join
    .unwrap;
```
## License and Links

- [Documentation](https://docs.rs/fragile/)
- [Issue Tracker](https://github.com/mitsuhiko/fragile/issues)
- License: [Apache 2.0](https://github.com/mitsuhiko/fragile/blob/master/LICENSE)

# async-trait 0.1.89 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/async-trait/^0.1.38

# Async trait methods

The stabilization of async functions in traits in Rust 1.75 did not include
support for using traits containing async functions as `dyn Trait`. Trying to
use dyn with an async trait produces the following error:

```
```
```
error[E0038]: the trait `Trait` is not dyn compatible
 --> src/main.rs:5:22
  |
5 | pub fn make() -> Box<dyn Trait> {
  |                      ^^^^^^^^^ `Trait` is not dyn compatible
  |
note: for a trait to be dyn compatible it needs to allow building a vtable
      for more information, visit <https://doc.rust-lang.org/reference/items/traits.html#dyn-compatibility>
 --> src/main.rs:2:14
  |
1 | pub trait Trait {
  |           ----- this trait is not dyn compatible...
2 |     async fn f(&self);
  |              ^ ...because method `f` is `async`
  = help: consider moving `f` to another trait
```
This crate provides an attribute macro to make async fn in traits work with dyn traits.

Please refer to [ why async fn in traits are hard](https://smallcultfollowing.com/babysteps/blog/2019/10/26/async-fn-in-traits-are-hard/) for a deeper analysis
of how this implementation differs from what the compiler and language deliver
natively.

## Example

This example implements the core of a highly effective advertising platform using async fn in a trait.

The only thing to notice here is that we write an `#[async_trait]` macro on top
of traits and trait impls that contain async fn, and then they work. We get to
have `Vec<Box<dyn Advertisement + Sync>>` or `&[&dyn Advertisement]`, for
example.

```
use async_trait;
;
```
## Supported features

It is the intention that all features of Rust traits should work nicely with
#[async_trait], but the edge cases are numerous. *Please file an issue if you
see unexpected borrow checker errors, type errors, or warnings.* There is no use
of `unsafe` in the expanded code, so rest assured that if your code compiles it
can't be that badly broken.

- 👍 Self by value, by reference, by mut reference, or no self;
- 👍 Any number of arguments, any return value;
- 👍 Generic type parameters and lifetime parameters;
- 👍 Associated types;
- 👍 Having async and non-async functions in the same trait;
- 👍 Default implementations provided by the trait;
- 👍 Elided lifetimes.

## Explanation

Async fns get transformed into methods that return `Pin<Box<dyn Future + Send + 'async_trait>>` and delegate to an async block.

For example the `impl Advertisement for AutoplayingVideo` above would be
expanded as:

```
```
## Non-threadsafe futures

Not all async traits need futures that are `dyn Future + Send`. To avoid having
Send and Sync bounds placed on the async trait methods, invoke the async trait
macro as `#[async_trait(?Send)]` on both the trait and the impl blocks.

## Elided lifetimes

Be aware that async fn syntax does not allow lifetime elision outside of `&` and
`&mut` references. (This is true even when not using #[async_trait].)
Lifetimes must be named or marked by the placeholder `'_`.

Fortunately the compiler is able to diagnose missing lifetimes with a good error message.

```
type Elided<'a> = &'a usize;
```
```
error[E0726]: implicit elided lifetime not allowed here
 --> src/main.rs:9:29
  |
9 |     async fn test(not_okay: Elided, okay: &usize) {}
  |                             ^^^^^^- help: indicate the anonymous lifetime: `<'_>`
```
The fix is to name the lifetime or use `'_`.

```
```

# auto_enums 0.8.9 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/auto_enums/^0.8.5

# auto_enums

A library for to allow multiple return types by automatically generated enum.

This crate is a procedural macro implementation of the features discussions
in [rust-lang/rfcs#2414](https://github.com/rust-lang/rfcs/issues/2414). This idea is also known as
["Anonymous sum types"](https://github.com/rust-lang/rfcs/issues/294).

This library provides the following attribute macros:

-
`#[auto_enum]`Parses syntax, creates the enum, inserts variants, and passes specified traits to `#[enum_derive]`.
-
`#[enum_derive]`Implements specified traits to the enum.

## Usage

Add this to your `Cargo.toml`:

```
[]
 = "0.8"
```
## Examples

`#[auto_enum]`'s basic feature is to wrap the value returned by the obvious
branches (`match`, `if`, `return`, etc..) by an enum that implemented the
specified traits.

```
use auto_enum;
```
`#[auto_enum]` generates code in two stages.

First, `#[auto_enum]` will do the following.

- parses syntax
- creates the enum
- inserts variants

Code like this will be generated:

```
```
Next, `#[enum_derive]` implements the specified traits.

`#[auto_enum]` can also parse nested arms/branches by using the `#[nested]`
attribute.

```
use auto_enum;
```
See [documentation](https://docs.rs/auto_enums) for more details.

## Supported traits

`#[enum_derive]` implements the supported traits and passes unsupported
traits to `#[derive]`.

`#[enum_derive]` supports many of the standard library traits and some popular
third-party libraries traits such as [rayon](https://docs.rs/rayon/1), [futures](https://docs.rs/futures/0.3),
[tokio](https://docs.rs/tokio/1), [http_body](https://docs.rs/http_body/1). **See  documentation for a complete list of supported traits.**

If you want to use traits that are not supported by `#[enum_derive]`, you
can use another crate that provides [derives macros](https://doc.rust-lang.org/reference/procedural-macros.html#derive-macros), or
you can define derives macros yourself ([derive_utils](https://github.com/taiki-e/derive_utils) probably can help it).

Basic usage of `#[enum_derive]`

```
use enum_derive;
// `#[enum_derive]` implements `Iterator`, and `#[derive]` implements `Clone`.
```

# auto_impl 1.3.0 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/auto_impl/^1.3.0

A proc-macro attribute for automatically implementing a trait for references, some common smart pointers and closures.

# Usage

This library requires Rust 1.56.0 or newer. This library doesn't leave any public API in your code.

Add `auto_impl` to your `Cargo.toml` and just use it in your crate:

```
// In Rust 2015 you still need `extern crate auto_impl;` at your crate root
use auto_impl;
```
Add an `auto_impl` attribute to traits you want to automatically implement for wrapper types. Here is a small example:

```
// This will generate two additional impl blocks: one for `&T` and one
// for `Box<T>` where `T: Foo`.
requires_foo;  // works: through the impl we defined above
requires_foo; // works: through the generated impl
requires_foo; // works: through the generated impl
```
For more explanations, please see [ the documentation](https://docs.rs/auto_impl) and for more examples, see

[the examples folder](https://github.com/auto-impl-rs/auto_impl/tree/master/examples).

# Alternatives

This library implements a fraction of a very broad and complex usecase. It's mostly useful for applications that
define traits for components, and want to be able to abstract over the storage for those traits. If it doesn't offer
some functionality you need, check out the [ impl-tools](https://github.com/kas-gui/impl-tools/) project.

# mockall_double 0.3.1 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/mockall_double/^0.3.1

# mockall_double

A double test adapter that works well with Mockall.

## Overview

Mockall can easily create a mock version of a struct.  But how does one
convince the code under test to use the mock struct instead of the real one?
In Rust, it's necessary to replace the real struct at compile time.  That's
very easy to do with a few `#[cfg(test)]` statements.  But mockall_double makes
it even easier.

## Usage

Typically `mockall` is only used by unit tests, so it can be a dev-dependency.
But `mockall_double` must be a full dependency.  To use it this way, add this to
your `Cargo.toml`:

```
[]
 = "0.3.1"
[]
 = "0.12.0"
```
Then use it like this:

```
use double;
use Foo;
```
See the [API docs](https://docs.rs/mockall_double) for more information.

# Minimum Supported Rust Version (MSRV)

`mockall_double` is tested with the same MSRV as Mockall itself.  Currently,
that's Rust 1.42.0.  `mockall_double`'s MSRV will not be changed in the future
without bumping the major or minor version.

# License

`mockall_double` is primarily distributed under the terms of both the MIT
license and the Apache License (Version 2.0).

See LICENSE-APACHE, and LICENSE-MIT for details

# Acknowledgements

`mockall_double` is inspired by Jason Grlicky's
[double](https://crates.io/crates/double) crate, but tweaked to work better
with Mockall's naming conventions.
